beats.scene: Mole in a rumpled gown tells his news eagerly to Badger, Rat and Toad
beats.summary: Mole reports, and Badger says they will strike that very night.

beats.scene: Badger hands out clubs, cutlasses and pistols to the friends by the fire
beats.summary: That evening Badger gives each friend weapons for the attack.

beats.scene: Toad lies on a sofa grumbling while Badger watches the clock
beats.summary: They rest for a few hours until dusk.

beats.scene: Four animals in single file walk along the dim river bank at dusk
beats.summary: At dusk the four friends set out along the river bank.

beats.scene: Badger pushes aside willow roots to reveal a dark hole in the bank
beats.summary: Badger finds the hidden entrance and they crawl in.

beats.scene: A dim lantern shows four animals bending low in a long dripping tunnel
beats.summary: The tunnel is long, low, cold and damp.

beats.scene: The friends crouch at the foot of rough steps below a trapdoor
beats.summary: The tunnel ends below a trapdoor, and they hear a roar of voices overhead.

beats.scene: Four friends crouch in the dark listening to a shouted speech above
beats.summary: They hear the Wild Wooders cheer a speech and sing mocking songs about Toad.

beats.scene: Toad shakes with fury as Badger grips his shoulder in the dark
beats.summary: Toad nearly bursts out, but Badger holds him back.

beats.scene: Badger whispers orders to three friends with his paw on the trapdoor
beats.summary: Badger whispers his final orders: they will burst in together at his signal.

beats.scene: Badger heaves open the trapdoor and light floods into the tunnel
beats.summary: Badger gives the signal and heaves the trapdoor open.

beats.scene: Four friends burst through a trapdoor into a banquet hall of startled weasels
beats.summary: The four burst into the banquet hall and the Wild Wooders panic.

beats.scene: Badger swings his club as weasels dive under the tables
beats.summary: Each friend fights in his own way: Badger roars, Rat and Mole charge, Toad shrieks.

beats.scene: Terrified weasels scramble through windows and under tables as chairs topple
beats.summary: The terrified weasels flee through windows and doors and even up the chimney.

beats.scene: The Chief Weasel shouts orders from a chair as his followers push past
beats.summary: The Chief Weasel tries to rally his followers, but nobody will listen.

beats.scene: Toad swings his club at a fleeing ferret while Mole ducks beside him
beats.summary: Toad, drunk with victory, chases weasels around the hall.

beats.scene: Weasel sentries flee across a dark lawn toward the gates
beats.summary: Outside, the sentries hear the din, imagine an army and run.

beats.scene: A few trembling weasels stand with raised paws before Badger
beats.summary: A few prisoners surrender, and Badger orders them to clean up and go.

beats.scene: Four friends stand panting in the wrecked hall, grinning at each other
beats.summary: The friends catch their breath and find that they have won, with only bruises.

beats.scene: Toad walks slowly through his wrecked rooms with a lamp in his paw
beats.summary: Toad walks through his damaged house and sees the mess the Wild Wooders left.

beats.scene: Four tired friends climb into soft beds in Toad Hall by candlelight
beats.summary: Exhausted, the friends go to sleep in the beds of Toad Hall.

beats.scene: Sunlight shines on a wrecked banqueting hall as four friends survey the damage
beats.summary: Next morning the friends see by daylight how much damage was done.

beats.scene: Toad's old servants carry brooms and buckets through the doors, smiling
beats.summary: Toad's old servants return and the cleaning begins.

beats.scene: Badger wags a finger at Toad beside a tall window in the evening light
beats.summary: Toad wants a banquet, and Badger warns him not to boast.

beats.scene: Toad scribbles on invitation cards, then crosses out his own lines
beats.summary: Toad starts a boastful invitation, then writes a modest one instead.

beats.scene: Toad seals parcels of presents for the people who helped him
beats.summary: Toad sends thanks and presents to those who helped him on his journey.

beats.scene: Lanterns glow in every window of a clean, bright Toad Hall as guests arrive
beats.summary: On the night of the banquet the Hall is spotless and the guests arrive.

beats.scene: Toad sits quietly at the table while guests laugh at Rat's tale
beats.summary: Toad keeps quiet, gives credit to his friends and is cheered.

beats.scene: Toad sits peacefully on the lawn while friends laugh nearby
beats.summary: From that evening Toad is quieter, kinder and wiser.

beats.scene: Weasel mothers whisper to small children beside a hole in the Wild Wood
beats.summary: The Wild Wooders learn to respect the friends.

beats.scene: Rat, Mole, Badger and Toad sit by the river at sunset in warm light
beats.summary: The friends settle into peaceful days and the book ends happily.

A1A2: Mole was tired of cleaning his house, so he threw down his brush.
He dug up through the earth, and soon he came out into the sun.
The meadow was warm, and the birds sang in the green hedge.
Soon he found a wide, bright river, and he had never seen one before.
On the other bank, a friendly face looked out of a small hole.
Mole sat in a boat for the first time, and he loved it.
Far away, Mole saw dark trees, and Rat told him about the Wild Wood.
Rat opened a big basket, and it was full of good food.
A friendly otter stopped to talk, but a shy badger hid away.
Mole tried to row, but the boat turned over and they fell in.
Rat pulled Mole out of the river, and he laughed kindly.
Rat swam after the basket and brought back all the food.
They walked along the bank to Rat's warm home in the bank.
Rat made a bright fire and gave Mole some dry clothes.
Rat said, “Stay with me, and I will teach you the river.”
That evening Rat told Mole about his rich friend Toad.
Next day they went by boat to the big, grand Toad Hall.
Toad ran across the lawn to welcome them with open arms.
Toad proudly showed them a new yellow caravan in the stable yard.
Toad begged his friends to come with him on the open road.
Next morning they packed the caravan, and Toad hurried them along.
The caravan moved slowly along a quiet country road in the sun.
At noon they stopped to eat, and Toad talked about his plans.
At night they camped, ate supper and looked at the stars.
In the morning Toad slept, and Rat and Mole made breakfast.
Suddenly a fast car came down the road, making a loud noise.
The horse was afraid, and the caravan fell over into the ditch.
Toad sat in the road and smiled at the cloud of dust.
Rat was angry, but Toad only said that he wanted a car.
Rat and Mole took the train home and left Toad at an inn.
Every morning Rat taught Mole how to row the boat.
Rat showed Mole how to swim in the warm, shallow water.
Rat showed Mole the birds, the fish and the plants of the river.
One evening Rat sat by the water and wrote a song about ducks.
Otter often visited them and talked about his young son Portly.
The summer days went by, and the farmers cut the hay.
In autumn the leaves turned yellow and fell into the river.
When winter came, Rat slept more, and Mole often felt alone.
Snow fell on the river bank, and the world turned white.
Mole asked Rat about Badger, but Rat said they must wait.
One cold afternoon Rat fell asleep, and Mole felt bored.
Mole left quietly and walked over the snowy fields alone.
Mole came to the Wild Wood and went in among the trees.
In a hole, Mole saw a small face with hard, bright eyes.
Then Mole heard a thin whistle behind him in the wood.
Mole was afraid, so he ran as fast as he could.
Mole found a hole in an old tree and hid inside.
Rat woke up and saw that Mole was not at home.
Rat went into the dark wood, and he was not afraid.
Rat found Mole in the tree, and Mole said he was sorry.
Snow began to fall, and Rat and Mole could not find the way.
They walked on in the deep snow, and Mole was very tired.
Mole fell over something hard and hurt his leg badly.
Under the snow, Rat found a mat and a small green door.
Rat pulled the bell, and they waited in the cold snow.
Badger opened the door and said, “Who is it this time?”
Badger took them to a big warm kitchen with a bright fire.
Rat told Badger the story, and Badger was kind to Mole.
Badger gave them a big supper, and they ate it all.
Badger asked about Toad, and Rat told him about the cars.
In the morning, two young hedgehogs were eating breakfast in the kitchen.
Badger said that a big city of people once stood there.
The people went away, and the trees grew over their houses.
Badger showed Mole his house, and Mole loved the long tunnels.
Mole said that nothing was better than a home underground.
Badger said, “I will show you a short way home.”
In the tunnel Badger said he would deal with Toad soon.
At the end of the tunnel, they saw the bright snow.
Rat and Mole walked home over the white fields.
At home Mole sat by the fire and thought about his old house.
The winter weeks went by, and Mole went for long walks.
One cold day Rat took Mole on a long walk.
At dusk they passed a village, and lights shone in the windows.
In a quiet lane Mole stopped, because he smelled something.
It was the smell of his old home, and it called to him.
Mole began to cry, but Rat was far ahead and did not hear.
Mole said it was his old home, and he wanted to go back.
Rat said they would find the house, even if it took all night.
Mole followed the smell along a hedge and over a ditch.
They went down a tunnel, and there was Mole's little front door.
Inside, the house was dark, cold and covered in dust.
Rat found a lamp and lit it, and the rooms came to life.
Mole sat down and cried, saying he was sorry to bring Rat.
Rat laughed and said, “Cheer up, Mole, we will soon fix this.”
Rat looked in the cupboard and found some fish, biscuits and a sausage.
Outside the door there was a noise of small feet.
Rat opened the door and saw little mice with lanterns.
Rat sent one mouse to the village to buy some supper.
The mice came back with food, and they all ate together.
Mole lay in his old bed, and he was very happy.
Toad kept crashing cars, so Badger said it was time to act.
At Toad Hall, Badger and Rat took Toad inside and took off his coat.
Toad cried and said he was sorry, but he would not promise.
They locked Toad in his room, and they watched him day and night.
Toad said he was ill, and Rat ran to get a doctor.
Toad climbed out of the window and ran away across the grass.
Toad went to an inn, ate lunch and saw a car outside.
Toad could not stop himself, so he took the car and drove away.
The police chased Toad, and in the end they caught him.
The judge said Toad must go to prison for twenty years.
In summer Otter came to say that little Portly was lost.
Otter waited by the river, and his friends promised to help.
They rowed up the river in the dark and called Portly's name.
The moon came up, and the river turned to silver.
Rat heard a sweet song, and he stopped rowing.
They followed the music, and the air smelled sweet.
They came to a small island and stepped onto the grass.
Mole felt something great and kind close by, and he shook.
They looked up and saw a kind god with Portly asleep beside him.
The god was gone, and they took Portly home to Otter.
Toad was in prison, deep inside an old stone castle.
Toad cried all day, and he missed his house and friends.
The jailer's daughter was kind, and she brought Toad some tea.
Toad told her about his grand house, and she listened.
She said her aunt washed the prison clothes, and she had a plan.
At first Toad said no, but then he said yes.
The aunt came, took Toad's money, and gave him her clothes.
Toad put on the dress and the bonnet, and he looked funny.
Toad walked past all the guards, and nobody stopped him.
Toad was free, and he hurried to the train station.
At the station, Toad had no money for a ticket.
The driver said, “Wash my shirts, and you can ride.”
Toad rode on the engine, and he felt happy and proud.
The driver saw another engine behind them, full of police.
Toad put coal on the fire as fast as he could.
The driver told Toad to jump off after the long tunnel.
Toad jumped off the train, and the police went past.
Toad slept in a hole in a tree, and he was cold.
Next day, Toad found a boat on the canal, pulled by a horse.
Toad washed badly, and the woman threw him into the canal.
Toad was angry, so he took the horse and rode away.
Toad sold the horse to a man for coins and a hot meal.
Toad ate a big breakfast and walked on with a happy heart.
Toad sang a song about how clever he was.
A car stopped, and the people in it offered Toad a ride.
Toad got in, took the wheel, and the car went very fast.
The car went off the road and fell into a pond.
The people were in the water, so Toad ran away.
For many days Toad hid in the day and walked at night.
At last Toad saw the river, and he thought of Rat.
In autumn the swallows gathered, and Rat watched them sadly.
Rat said that he wanted to go south with the birds.
Rat went for a walk along the dusty road by himself.
On the road, Rat met a tired sailor and took him home.
The Sea Rat told stories about ships and the sea.
He told them about sunny ports and sweet fruit.
The Sea Rat said that the sea called anyone who heard it.
The Sea Rat thanked them and left for the sea.
Rat packed a bag, and he said he was going south.
Mole stood at the door and held Rat back with all his strength.
Mole gave Rat a drink and spoke kindly to him.
Mole gave Rat a pencil, and Rat began to write a poem.
Rat was soon himself again, and the two friends were happy.
One wet night, someone knocked loudly at Rat's door.
It was Toad, and he looked very dirty and tired.
By the fire, Toad began to tell them how clever he was.
Rat told Toad he was being silly and that things were bad.
Bad animals from the Wild Wood now lived in Toad Hall.
Toad shouted that he would fight them, but Rat stopped him.
Toad cried, and Rat said they must ask Badger for help.
The next day, Badger came and looked hard at Toad.
Badger spoke sternly, and then he shook Toad's paw.
Rat told Badger how many animals guarded Toad Hall.
Badger said he knew a secret way into the Hall.
Badger said a secret tunnel ran from the river to the Hall.
Mole said he would go and look, dressed as a washerwoman.
Mole walked up to Toad Hall in a dress and a bonnet.
The guards laughed and talked about a big party that night.
Mole saw many animals going into the Hall, and he left.
Mole told his news, and Badger said, “We go tonight.”
In the evening, Badger gave each friend a stick and a sword.
They rested until night, because Badger said it was wise.
At dusk the four friends walked along the river in a line.
Badger found a hole in the bank, and they went in.
The tunnel was long, dark and cold, but they kept walking.
At the end, they heard loud noise from above their heads.
They heard the weasels laughing and making jokes about Toad.
Toad was so angry that he wanted to shout.
Badger said, “When I shout, we all go up together.”
Badger gave a loud shout, and they pushed open the trapdoor.
The four friends jumped into the hall, and the weasels screamed.
Badger shouted loudly and swung his stick at the weasels.
The weasels ran away through the windows and the doors.
The Chief Weasel shouted, but nobody listened to him.
Toad ran after the weasels, shouting, “I am the Terror!”
The guards outside heard the noise and ran away.
A few weasels were caught, and Badger sent them to work.
The four friends stood in the hall and smiled at each other.
Toad walked through his house and saw the mess.
They were very tired, so they went to bed.
In the morning, the friends saw how much work there was.
Toad's servants came back, and everyone began to clean.
Toad wanted a big party, but Badger said, “No boasting.”
Toad wrote a card, crossed it out and wrote another.
Toad sent gifts to the kind people who had helped him.
On the night of the party, the Hall was clean and bright.
Toad was quiet, and he thanked his friends one by one.
From that day, Toad was quieter, kinder and wiser.
The Wild Wood animals learned to respect Badger and his friends.
The four friends lived happily near the river for many years.
B1B2: All morning Mole had scrubbed and swept his little home under the ground, and he was tired of it. At last he said “Bother, hang spring-cleaning,” and threw his brush across the room.
He ran to the narrow tunnel that led up to the surface and began to scrabble at the earth with his paws. At last his nose poked out into the open air, and he tumbled onto the warm grass.
Mole lay in the meadow for a while, feeling as if he had just been let out of prison. Then he trotted along the hedge, where the rabbits shouted rude jokes at him, but he was far too happy to mind.
Soon he came to a broad, shining river, which he had never seen in all his life. It slid along, chuckling and gurgling, and Mole sat on the bank, quite under its spell.

While he sat there, he noticed a small dark hole in the opposite bank, and a pair of bright eyes shone out of it. Then a whiskered face appeared, and a sleek Water Rat said, “Hullo, Mole,” as if they were old friends.
Mole had never been in a boat before, and every moment of it delighted him. “Believe me, there is nothing half so good as messing about in boats,” said Rat, “and the river is all I need.”
Beyond the meadows Mole saw a long, dark line of trees, and he asked what lay behind them. Rat said it was the Wild Wood, a place the river animals avoided, because weasels and stoats lived there.

They tied the boat under a shady bank, and Rat opened a large wicker basket packed with cold chicken, ham, pickles, salad and sandwiches. “Oh stop,” said Mole happily, “this is too much,” while Rat went on unpacking lemonade and ginger beer.

While they ate, an otter strolled along the bank and joined them for a chat, as if he had known Mole for years. Then a striped head peeped out of the hedge, muttered “Company,” and vanished, and Rat explained that Badger hated visitors.

After lunch Mole, full of confidence, begged to be allowed to row, although Rat warned him that he was not ready. He jumped up and grabbed the oars, and the boat promptly tipped over and threw them both into the river.
Rat jumped in at once and pulled the wet and frightened Mole safely onto the bank. Instead of being cross, he laughed and said that nobody minded a little water, because the river was their friend.
Then Rat dived again and again, and he rescued the floating hamper, the cushions and both oars. He turned the boat the right way up, and soon everything was on the bank, wet but safe.
Rat led his shivering friend along the bank to a neat little hole just above the water. Inside it was dry and clean, and Mole, who loved good houses, was charmed at once.
Rat lit a bright fire, wrapped Mole in a dressing gown and sat him in a deep armchair. Soon the steam rose from his fur, and Mole began to feel like himself again.
Mole thanked Rat for his kindness and said it had been the happiest day of his life. Rat answered that Mole should stay with him for a while, and that he would soon teach him to row and even to swim.

At supper they talked about the animals of the river bank, and Rat spoke warmly of his friend Toad. Toad, he explained, was rich and good-natured, but he was also vain, boastful and always chasing some new craze.
Next morning Rat rowed Mole upstream, and this time Mole sat still and did not touch the oars. Round the bend stood a fine old house of red brick, which Rat said was Toad Hall.
Toad came bounding across the lawn, shook their paws warmly and praised the lovely day. Boating, he said, was last year's fashion, and he had found something far, far better.

Toad led them to the stable yard, where a gipsy caravan stood, painted bright yellow with red and green wheels. Inside were little bunks, a tiny table, a cooking stove, a bookcase and even a cage with a canary.

Toad described the open road, the villages, the fields and the freedom of the traveller, until Mole could hardly keep still. Although Rat was stubborn at first, he saw how excited Mole was, and in the end he gave way.

Next morning Toad bustled about, giving orders, while Rat and Mole packed food, blankets and pans into the lockers. When at last the cream-coloured horse was harnessed, the caravan rolled out of the gate, and Toad's servants waved goodbye.

All morning the caravan creaked along quiet lanes between tall hedges, and the dust rose in little clouds behind it. Toad walked at the horse's head, singing his own praises, while Rat and Mole enjoyed the sunshine and the smell of the fields.
At noon they stopped under a spreading tree to eat and rest. Toad told them about the wonderful places they would visit, although in truth he had no idea where the road would lead.

That evening they stopped on a quiet common, where the horse was set free to graze. After supper the three friends sat on the caravan steps and watched the stars come out, and Toad talked about his adventures to come.

Next morning Toad stayed in his bunk, so Rat and Mole fed the horse, fetched water and cooked breakfast. When Toad finally appeared, he praised the lovely morning and said nothing at all about the work they had done.

They were walking quietly along the white road when they heard a faint “Poop-poop” behind them. A cloud of dust rolled closer, and a great motor car roared past, so fast that the three friends could hardly see it.

The horse reared up in terror and plunged sideways, and the caravan crashed into the ditch with a terrible noise. Rat shook his fist at the vanishing car and shouted that the driver was a villain who ought to be arrested.

Toad did not seem to mind at all, but sat down in the middle of the road with a faraway look in his eyes. “The poetry of motion,” he whispered, “that is the real way to travel,” and he murmured “poop-poop” again and again.
Rat tried to make Toad get up and help, but Toad only gazed at the sky and said the caravan was rubbish. Nothing mattered to him now, he declared, because he was going to buy a motor car.

At last they walked on to the nearest town, where they left the horse at an inn and arranged for the caravan to be fetched. Toad stayed behind in a trance, and Rat and Mole took the train home, sad that the holiday had ended so soon.
Every morning Rat took Mole out in the boat and showed him how to hold the oars. Mole's paws were sore at first, but he practised patiently, and before long he could row a straight line.
On hot afternoons Rat taught Mole to swim in the shallow water near the bank. Mole splashed and spluttered and swallowed a good deal of the river, but soon he learned to float on his back and kick.

Rat taught Mole to recognise the creatures of the river, from the bright blue kingfisher to the busy moorhens in the reeds. Soon Mole could tell one water plant from another, and he knew where the fat fish liked to rest.
One golden evening Rat sat on the bank with a pencil, watching the ducks dabble in the shallows. He was writing a song about them, and he kept humming it while Mole listened with admiration.
Otter often stopped by for a chat, and he told long, funny stories about the river. He spoke proudly of his small son Portly, who was just learning to swim and could not stay out of mischief.

The long summer days slipped by, one after another, and the farmers cut the hay and gathered in the golden corn. In the evenings Mole and Rat walked through the fields and watched the last of the harvest carts rumble home.
Then autumn came, and the leaves turned yellow and brown and drifted down onto the water. The hedges were heavy with berries, the mornings grew cool, and the evenings began earlier every day.
When the first frosts came, many animals went to sleep for the winter, and Rat grew sleepy too. He dozed by the fire for hours, and Mole, who was wide awake, sometimes felt rather lonely.
Soon the snow came, and the river bank lay silent and white beneath a pale sky. Mole stood at the window and stared across the fields toward the dark line of the Wild Wood.
Mole asked whether they might visit Badger, since he lived so near and sounded so interesting. Rat shook his head and said that Badger would never be hurried, and that they must wait for him to call.
One cold afternoon Rat fell asleep in his chair with a half-finished poem on his knee. Mole watched the dying fire for a while, and then he made up his mind to do something bold.
Mole put on his coat and slipped quietly out of the door, leaving Rat asleep. The air was cold and sharp, and he crossed the frozen fields toward the Wild Wood with the snow crunching under his feet.
At last Mole reached the edge of the Wild Wood, where the bare trees stood black against the white snow. He stepped between them, and at once the light grew dim and everything seemed strangely quiet.
Suddenly Mole saw a small, narrow face looking at him out of a hole between two roots. It vanished at once, but soon he noticed other faces, and each pair of hard, bright eyes was watching him.
Then he heard a thin, sharp whistle somewhere behind him, and another answered it far ahead. After that came a soft pattering, like the sound of many small feet, and it seemed to come from all sides.

Mole could bear it no longer, and he ran blindly through the trees with his heart pounding. Twigs lashed his face, roots caught his feet, and the whistling and pattering seemed to follow wherever he turned.
At last he saw a hollow at the foot of a great old tree, and he scrambled into it, trembling. He lay still among the dry leaves, listening, while the whistles and footsteps went on and on outside.

Meanwhile Rat woke up by the fire and called for Mole, but nobody answered. Seeing small footprints in the snow, he guessed the truth, took his pistols and a stout stick, and hurried after his friend.

Rat followed the tracks into the Wild Wood without a trace of fear, and he even whistled as he walked. The hidden faces watched him from their holes, but when they saw his pistols, they drew back and let him pass.

At last Rat found Mole shivering in the hollow tree, and he crawled in beside him. Mole said he had been foolish and begged to be forgiven, and Rat patted him gently and said that everyone gets frightened sooner or later.

Soon big flakes were whirling through the trees, and the ground vanished beneath a thick white blanket. Rat looked around anxiously and admitted that every path had disappeared, and that they could not tell which way led home.
They struggled on through the deep drifts, but every tree looked the same as the last. Mole was so tired that he could hardly lift his feet, and Rat had to encourage him at every step.

Suddenly Mole tripped over something hard and fell headlong into the snow, crying out that his leg was hurt. Rat knelt beside him, examined the leg carefully, and then began to scratch at the snow with great interest.

“Mole, you are a wonder,” said Rat joyfully, because the thing that had cut his leg was an iron scraper for wiping boots. They dug furiously, and soon they uncovered a doormat, and behind it a solid green door in the bank.
The brass plate said Mr Badger, and Rat gave the bell-pull a long, hard tug. A deep clang rang out far inside the hill, and the two friends waited, shivering, in the falling snow.
The door opened a crack, and a long snout and a pair of sleepy eyes looked out. “The next time this happens, I shall be very angry,” said a gruff voice, “so who is it now, on such a night?”
Badger led them down a long passage lit by a single lamp and into a large, warm kitchen. Hams hung from the ceiling, a bright fire burned in the hearth, and two comfortable benches waited beside it.

Rat told Badger the whole story, while Mole stared into the fire and felt rather ashamed. Badger listened gravely and said that he would not scold anyone, because a stormy night was no time for lectures.

Badger laid the table and fetched cold meat, pickles, bread and cheese, and the two travellers ate hungrily. Between mouthfuls, Mole began to feel that the terrors of the Wild Wood belonged to another world.

After supper Badger asked for news of the river, and Rat told him how Toad was crashing one motor car after another. Badger shook his head gloomily and said that something must be done, though not until the new year.

Next morning Rat and Mole came downstairs and found two young hedgehogs eating porridge at the kitchen table. The little animals jumped up politely, for they had lost their way in the snow and Badger had given them shelter for the night.
After breakfast Badger sat by the fire and told them a strange tale. Long ago, he said, there had been a great city of people on the very ground where the Wild Wood now stood.
Then the people left, the rains fell and the wind blew, and the forest slowly covered the ruined city. Many animals found shelter in its old halls, and their families have lived there ever since.

Badger showed Mole round his house, with its stone halls, long passages and store rooms full of apples, nuts and honey. Mole, who had always been fond of underground homes, said that he had never seen one so fine.

Mole said that nothing could be as safe and snug as a home below the ground, where no storm could reach you. Badger beamed, for this was what he believed himself, and he decided that he liked Mole very much.
When it was time to leave, Badger said that he knew a short way home that ran right under the Wild Wood. He lit a lantern and led them into a long, narrow tunnel that went on and on beneath the hill.

As they walked, Badger told them that the Wild Wooders were not so bad when treated firmly, and that they gave him no trouble. Then he promised that he would deal with Toad in the new year, whether Toad liked it or not.
At last the tunnel ended in a small hole hidden by bushes, and the friends crept out into the bright winter light. Badger said goodbye, told them to come again soon, and went back into the darkness.

The two friends walked home across the glittering fields, and the cold air made their cheeks tingle. Mole said little, but he was thinking that he had learned two lessons, one about the Wild Wood and one about friends.

Back in Rat's warm house, Mole ate a good supper and stretched his toes toward the fire. Although he was very happy there, he suddenly found himself thinking about the little home he had left in the spring.
The winter weeks slipped by, and Rat spent most of his days dozing beside the fire. Mole took long walks along the frozen bank, and the memory of his old home came back to him more and more often.

One crisp afternoon Rat said that they both needed some fresh air, and he led Mole across the frozen fields. They walked briskly for hours, talking and laughing, and the pale sun sank slowly behind the hills.
As dusk fell, they passed through a village, where yellow light glowed behind every window. Mole peered at the cosy rooms and imagined the families gathered round their tables and their fires.
Beyond the village they walked along a frosty lane, and suddenly Mole stopped dead. A faint, familiar smell had drifted across the cold air, and it made his heart leap.

It was the smell of his own old home, the home he had left in the first rush of spring. It seemed to call him through the dark as plainly as a voice, and it pulled at his heart until tears ran down his face.

Rat, who was walking on ahead, did not notice for several minutes, and then he turned around in alarm. He found Mole shaking with sobs in the middle of the road, and he put an arm gently round his shoulders.
Mole explained that it was the smell of his old home, a poor little place that he had not thought of for months. He knew it was shabby, he said, but it was his own, and it was calling him back.
Rat said at once that they must go and find the house, even if it took them all night. “Come along, old fellow,” he said, “follow your nose, and I will follow you.”

Mole sniffed the air, turned down a narrow path and led Rat along a hedge, over a stile and across a frozen ditch. The smell grew stronger with every step, until at last he stopped beside a bank and cried, “Here it is.”

They crawled down a narrow tunnel, and at its end stood a small front door with a name painted over it. The name was Mole End, and when Mole saw it, he began to cry again, though this time he was smiling.
Inside, Mole End was cold and dark, and thick dust lay on every chair and shelf. Mole stood in the doorway and stared at the cobwebs, and he felt ashamed that Rat should see his poor house like this.
Rat found a lamp on the table and lit it, and the little rooms glowed softly in its light. Everything stood where Mole had left it, but a thick coat of dust covered it all.
Mole sank into a chair and wept, saying that he should never have brought Rat to such a dreary place. There was no fire, no food and no welcome, and he felt that he had spoiled the whole evening.
Rat laughed and told him not to be silly, and then he went about lighting lamps and poking at the ashes. Soon a small fire was crackling, and the chilly room began to look almost welcoming.
Rat rummaged through the cupboards and soon announced that he had found a tin of sardines, a box of biscuits and even a sausage. “That is a banquet,” he said, “for two hungry travellers.”
Just then they heard a shuffling of many small feet outside the door, and a soft sound of whispering. A voice said, “Now then, one two three,” and a tiny choir began to sing.

Rat flung open the door, and there stood a ring of little field mice with red scarves and lanterns in their paws. They were singing a carol about the frosty season, and their small, clear voices filled the passage.

Mole asked the singers to come in, and they crowded round the fire, warming their paws on hot drinks. Rat put some coins in the paw of the eldest mouse and sent him to the village to buy a good supper.

Soon the mouse returned with a basket of cold meat, bread and good things, and the little table was filled. They all ate merrily, and Mole, sitting at the head of the table, felt like a proper host again.

When the mice had said goodnight and gone, Mole climbed into his own old bed and pulled the blanket up to his chin. He knew now that he loved the river and Rat's house, but that nothing could replace the place that was his own.
All winter, bad news came from Toad Hall: he had bought several motor cars and wrecked every one. At last Badger himself appeared at Rat's door and said that the time had come to take Toad in hand.

Toad stood in goggles and an enormous coat beside a huge new car, and he invited them for a spin. Badger and Rat seized him, marched him into the house and took off his driving clothes while he kicked and shouted.

Badger talked to Toad seriously for a long time, and Toad cried and seemed truly sorry. But when Badger asked him to promise never to drive again, Toad suddenly refused, saying that he did not mean to give up motor cars.
Badger said that Toad must be locked in his bedroom until he came to his senses. The three friends moved into the Hall and took turns to sit outside his door, day and night.
When it was Rat's turn to keep watch, Toad began to groan and said he was dying. Rat, who was kind-hearted, did not quite believe him, but he locked the door again and hurried away to fetch a doctor.

As soon as Rat was gone, Toad jumped out of bed, tied his sheets together and climbed down from the window. He ran away across the park, laughing at his own cleverness, and he did not stop until he reached the road.
Toad walked to an inn called the Red Lion, where he ordered a large lunch and ate it with great enjoyment. Then he wandered out into the yard, and there stood a shiny motor car with nobody near it.
Toad told himself that he would only look at the car, and then that he would only sit in it. In the end he started the engine and roared off down the road, singing at the top of his voice.
Toad raced through villages and scattered hens and ducks in every direction. Before long the police were chasing him, and at the end of the lane two strong policemen seized him by the collar.

In court, the stern old judge listed Toad's crimes: stealing a motor car, driving furiously and being rude to the police. The clerk added up the sentences, and the judge said, “Make it twenty years,” and Toad was led away.
One hot evening in midsummer, Otter came to Rat's door looking worried and pale. His small son Portly had been missing since the morning, and he had searched everywhere without finding him.
Otter said he would keep watch at the shallow ford, where Portly had first learned to swim. Rat and Mole promised to search the river with the boat, and they set out as the sun went down.

They rowed upstream in the failing light, calling Portly's name along the banks and peering into every hole. Nobody answered them, but they would not give up, and the darkness slowly settled over the water.
At last the moon rose, large and round, and it turned the whole river to silver. Everything seemed strangely still, as though the night itself were holding its breath.
Suddenly Rat stopped rowing and lifted his head, as if he were listening to something far away. “Do you hear it,” he whispered, “the most beautiful tune I have ever heard?”

Rat steered the boat toward the music as if he were in a dream, and Mole could only follow. The air grew sweet with the scent of roses and meadowsweet, and the colours of the banks seemed brighter than by day.

Before long they heard the soft roar of a weir, and they saw a small island lying in the middle of the stream. They tied the boat to a willow root and stepped onto the grass, which was wet and sweet with dew.

In a green clearing Mole felt a great, gentle presence close by, and he began to tremble from head to foot. Rat, too, was shaking, and he whispered that he was afraid and yet not afraid, for he sensed that this power wished them only good.
They looked up and saw Pan, the great god of wild things, with curved horns and kind, smiling eyes. Between his hooves lay little Portly, fast asleep and perfectly safe.
When the sun rose, the vision faded, and a gentle gift of forgetfulness came to them on the breeze. They lifted Portly into the boat, rowed home and gave him to his happy father.
Toad was taken to the strongest prison in the land, an ancient castle with thick walls and heavy doors. He was led down many steps into a dark dungeon, and the key turned with a hollow clang.
Toad threw himself on the stone floor and cried for hours, thinking of his comfortable home and his clever friends. Twenty years was so long that he would be an old toad when he came out.

The jailer had a kind-hearted daughter who loved animals, and she felt very sorry for the miserable prisoner. One evening she brought him a tray with hot tea and buttered toast, and Toad began to cheer up.
She asked him to tell her about his famous house, and Toad was happy to boast again. He described the lawns, the boathouse and the grand dining room, and she listened with wide, admiring eyes.

Then the girl said quietly that she would like to help him, because her aunt was the prison washerwoman. Every Monday the old lady came to collect the washing, and the girl had thought of a clever plan.
When she explained her plan, Toad was shocked, for he was far too grand to dress as a washerwoman. After a moment's thought, however, he saw that it was his only hope, and he gave in.
On Monday the old aunt came with her basket, and Toad gave her every coin in his purse. She was glad to help, and she handed over her gown, her apron, her shawl and her bonnet.

Toad put on the gown, the apron, the shawl and the bonnet, and the girl tied the strings under his chin. When he looked at himself, he saw that he made a most convincing washerwoman, round and stout and respectable.

Toad walked along the dark corridors with his basket, and each guard he passed wished him goodnight. One of them even made a joke about the washing, and Toad had to bite his tongue to stop himself from answering.
Outside the gate, Toad felt the cool night air on his face and almost danced for joy. He hurried down the hill toward the lights of the town, hoping to catch a train that would take him home.

At the station a train stood waiting, puffing steam, but Toad searched his pockets and found that he had no money at all. He stood on the platform feeling helpless, and for the first time he wished that he had kept a coin or two.
Toad told the engine driver a sad story about a poor washerwoman who had lost her money. The kind driver said that if she would wash a few of his shirts, she might ride on the engine for nothing.

Soon the train was thundering through the dark countryside, and Toad stood proudly on the engine, laughing at the wind. He was so happy that he forgot his bonnet, and he began to boast to the driver about his adventures.

Just then the driver looked back and saw another engine racing after them, with policemen waving from its cab. He said that Toad had told a fine story, but that he had never liked policemen, so he would try to help.

Toad grabbed a shovel and heaped coal on the fire, and the engine roared faster and faster through the night. Behind them the police engine fell back a little, but its whistle still screamed in the darkness.
Ahead lay a long tunnel, and the driver told Toad what to do. As soon as they came out, he would slow the engine, and Toad must jump off and hide in the wood beside the line.

When the engine slowed, Toad jumped off and rolled down the bank into the long grass. He lay there, holding his breath, while the police engine thundered past in the darkness, and then he crept away into the wood.
It was a long, cold night in the wood, and Toad heard strange noises all around him. At last he found a hollow tree, curled up in it and fell asleep, dreaming of Toad Hall.
In the morning Toad woke up stiff and hungry and made his way to a canal, where a horse was pulling a barge. A stout woman at the back called out kindly and asked if he would like to come on board.

Toad had never washed anything in his life, and he soon made a terrible mess of the woman's clothes. When she laughed at him, he lost his temper and shouted that he was Toad, and she threw him into the canal.
Toad scrambled out of the water, dripping and furious, while the woman laughed at him from the deck. He ran along the towpath, unhooked the horse from its rope, jumped on its back and galloped away.
After a long gallop Toad came to a gipsy sitting beside a fire, with a pot of stew bubbling over it. The gipsy liked the look of the horse, and Toad sold it for a few coins and a huge hot breakfast.

Toad ate stew until he could eat no more, and then he set off again along the white road, feeling stronger and happier. The sun was warm, the coins jingled in his pocket, and he began to think he was the cleverest toad alive.

As he walked, Toad thought over his escapes, and he grew prouder and prouder with every step. By the end of the lane he was singing a song about himself, which said that no prison could hold such a clever toad.

Soon he heard a familiar “Poop-poop” behind him, and a large motor car slowed down beside him. The kind people inside offered the old washerwoman a lift, and Toad felt a strange thrill go through him.
Toad climbed in and sat quietly for a while, but his fingers soon began to twitch. Then he jumped up, pushed the driver aside, seized the wheel and shouted that he was Toad, the famous driver.
The car shot forward faster and faster, swerved across the road, ran through a hedge and plunged into a pond. Toad flew out of his seat, sailed through the air and landed on the grass of the meadow.

The owners of the car climbed out of the pond, dripping and shouting, and they ran after Toad across the meadow. Toad lifted his skirts, put his head down and ran faster than he had ever run in his life.
For many days after that, Toad hid in ditches and haystacks by day and crept along the lanes by night. He was dirty, hungry and tired, and his proud songs were quite forgotten.

At last Toad saw the willows and the silver gleam of his own river in the distance, and tears came to his eyes. He decided to knock at Rat's door, because Rat was the only friend who might still take him in.
Meanwhile on the river bank, summer had faded into autumn, and the swallows were gathering on the roofs and wires. Rat watched them with a restless feeling, though he could not say why.

One day Mole asked what was troubling him, and Rat said quietly that the swallows were leaving for the south. He added that he sometimes wished he could follow them, just to see the lands that they knew.
Rat decided to walk along the high road to shake off his restless mood. The highway was dusty and silent, and it ran away to the south as far as he could see.
On the road Rat met a weather-beaten stranger, a lean grey rat with a gold earring. The stranger said he was a Sea Rat from the southern ports, and Rat gladly invited him home for a meal.

Over lunch the Sea Rat told them about his life on the ships, the storms and the long weeks when there was nothing but water. Rat and Mole listened without eating, for his stories were more exciting than any dinner.

He described the southern harbours, where the water was blue, the houses were white and the markets were full of oranges and figs. In the evenings, he said, the fishermen sang, and their boats came home with the sunset.
The Sea Rat leaned closer and said that anyone who had once heard the sea could never forget it. Rat sat very still, and his eyes grew dreamy, as if he could already see the white sails.

At last the Sea Rat stood up, thanked them and said that he must go at once, because the tide waited for nobody. Rat followed him to the door and watched him walk away down the road, a small figure carrying a pack.
Rat did not seem to hear Mole's questions, and he began to fill a satchel with food and clothes. He said he was going south to the sea, and he did not know if he would ever come back.
Mole stood in the doorway, took hold of his friend with both paws and refused to let him pass. Rat struggled wildly for a time, but at last his strength gave out and he sank to the floor, trembling.

Mole helped Rat into his armchair, gave him a drink and spoke to him softly until he stopped shaking. Then Rat said in a tired voice that he had been under a spell, and that he was glad Mole had stopped him.
Mole was wise and did not argue, but he put a pencil and some paper into Rat's paws. Rat began to write, slowly at first, and soon the verses were flowing and his mind was far happier.

In the days that followed, Rat grew more cheerful, and the strange longing faded away. The two friends spent cosy evenings by the fire, and Rat read his new poems aloud while Mole listened and nodded.
One wet and windy night, the friends were about to go to bed when someone knocked at the door. Rat opened it, and in the light of the lamp he saw a bent, muddy, dripping figure.
Then Rat gasped, because under the mud and the rags he recognised the face of his old friend. It was Toad, thin and weary, and he asked in a feeble voice whether he might come in.
Rat gave Toad dry clothes, a hot meal and a chair by the fire, and Toad soon felt better. Almost at once he began to boast about his daring escapes and how cleverly he had fooled everyone.

Rat said sternly that there was nothing to be proud of, because Toad had been a fool from beginning to end. Then he told him the truth, that while he was away, a terrible thing had happened to Toad Hall.

Rat explained that the weasels, stoats and ferrets of the Wild Wood had driven out the servants and taken over Toad Hall. They had been living there for weeks, eating Toad's food, sleeping in his beds and laughing at his misfortune.

Toad jumped to his feet and shouted that he would drive the thieves out single-handed. Rat pulled him back into his chair and said that there were far too many of them and that every gate was guarded.

At last Toad sat down and wept, saying that he was the most foolish animal alive. Rat and Mole looked at each other, and Rat said that in the morning they would send for Badger, who always knew what to do.
Next morning Badger arrived at Rat's house and looked at Toad for a long time without speaking. Toad hung his head, for he knew that Badger had every right to say a great many things.

At last Badger told Toad that he had been a great fool, and that all his troubles were his own fault. But then he shook Toad's paw kindly and said that the past was past, and that they must think about the future.

Rat told Badger all he knew about the Wild Wooders in Toad Hall, and how they kept guards at every gate. Badger listened, nodding slowly, and then he asked Toad to draw a rough plan of the house and the grounds.
Badger studied the plan and said that they could never win by force, since the Wild Wooders were too many. Then he smiled and added that he knew something about Toad Hall that nobody else remembered.

Badger told them about a secret passage that began near the river bank and ran right under the grounds into Toad Hall. Toad's father had shown it to him long ago, and he had made Badger promise to keep it secret.
Badger said they needed to know what the Wild Wooders were doing inside the Hall. Mole bravely offered to go and look, wearing Toad's old gown and bonnet as a disguise.

Mole walked to Toad Hall with a basket on his arm, and he looked so much like a harmless washerwoman that nobody suspected him. At the gate, two stoats with sticks stepped out and demanded to know who he was and what he wanted.

The stoats laughed at the idea of a washerwoman in such a place and told her to go round to the kitchen door. As Mole turned away, he heard them say that the Chief Weasel was giving a great banquet in the hall that very night.

From a quiet corner of the garden Mole saw lights in every window and crowds of weasels and ferrets hurrying toward the front door. He slipped away through the hedge, delighted with what he had learned.

Mole hurried back and told his friends everything he had seen, and they listened eagerly. Badger rubbed his paws together and said that no better chance would ever come, because they would all be busy feasting.
That evening Badger opened a cupboard and gave each of the friends a stout club, a cutlass and a pair of pistols. Toad swung his club wildly, and Badger told him sternly to stand back.
Badger made them all rest on the sofas until dusk, because he said that tired soldiers lose battles. Toad could not stop talking, and he kept sitting up to describe how bravely he would fight.

At dusk Badger woke them, and the four friends crept out of the house and followed the river bank in single file. Not a word was spoken, and the only sounds were the water, the wind and their quiet footsteps.

Not far from Toad's boathouse, Badger stopped beside an old willow and pushed aside a curtain of roots. Behind it was a narrow hole that nobody would ever have noticed, and one by one they crawled in.
The tunnel was low and damp, and water dripped from the roof onto their heads. They had to bend almost double, and they walked for what felt like hours in the dim light of the lantern.
At last the tunnel came to a short flight of steps, and above them they could see the outline of a trapdoor. From the room above came a muffled roar of voices, laughter and the clatter of plates.
They heard the Chief Weasel making a speech about how clever the Wild Wooders had been, and the crowd cheered every word. Then someone began a rude song about Toad, and all the others joined in.

Toad shook with rage, and for a moment he looked as if he would burst through the trapdoor alone. Badger gripped his shoulder and whispered a warning, and Toad swallowed his anger with a great effort.
Badger whispered his last orders to the three friends in the darkness. When he gave the signal, they must all burst up through the trapdoor together, shouting as loudly as they could.

Badger drew a deep breath, shouted the signal and heaved the trapdoor open with his strong back. A blaze of light and noise rushed down at them, and the four friends sprang up the steps into the hall.

The four friends burst up through the floor, shouting at the top of their voices, and the weasels dropped their forks in terror. Tables fell over, plates smashed, and the whole hall rang with screams.

Badger roared like a lion and swung his club, while Rat and Mole charged forward with their cutlasses. Toad leaped about on the tables, waving his club and shouting that he was the terror of the river.
The weasels fled in all directions, through the windows, under the tables and even up the chimney. In the confusion each one thought that he alone was being attacked by a hundred enemies.
The Chief Weasel tried to rally his followers, shouting that they were far more numerous than their enemies. But nobody listened, and he was swept toward the door by the stream of running animals.
Toad ran wildly about the hall, whacking at every tail he could reach and shouting his own name in a terrible voice. Mole had to duck twice, and Badger called out that it was time to calm down.

Outside the Hall the sentries heard the uproar and thought that a huge army was attacking. They threw down their sticks and ran for the gates, and the last of the Wild Wooders disappeared into the dark.
A few weasels had been too frightened to run, and they stood with their paws in the air, begging for mercy. Badger told them sternly to clean up the mess and then leave Toad Hall and never come back.
When it was all over, the four friends stood in the middle of the wrecked hall, panting and grinning at each other. Nobody was hurt except for a few bruises, and the Hall was theirs again.
Toad walked slowly through his own rooms, looking at the broken plates, the torn curtains and the dirty footprints on the carpet. He was sad, but also deeply glad to be back, and he said so out loud.
Badger said that they all needed sleep, and that the cleaning could wait until tomorrow. The four friends climbed into clean beds, and soon the only sounds in Toad Hall were snores.
In the morning the friends came downstairs and saw the Hall by daylight. It was worse than they had thought, with broken windows, burnt carpets and mountains of dirty plates.
News of the victory spread, and by noon Toad's old servants came hurrying back from their hiding places. They brought brooms, buckets and cheerful faces, and the long job of cleaning began.
Toad suggested a grand banquet to thank all his friends, and Badger agreed, on one condition. There must be no boasting, no long speeches and no songs about how clever Toad had been.
Toad sat down to write the invitations, and the first one was full of grand words about himself. Then he remembered Badger's rule, tore it up and wrote a plain, friendly card instead.

Toad remembered the kind people who had helped him, and he sent thank-you letters and presents to the jailer's daughter and the engine driver. He was surprised to find how good it felt to be grateful.

On the night of the banquet, Toad Hall was clean and bright again, with lanterns glowing in every window. Otter, Portly, the hedgehogs, the field mice and many other friends arrived to join the celebration.

During the dinner Toad said very little, and he even turned down a chance to make a long speech. He thanked Badger, Rat and Mole by name, and said that they had saved his home and taught him a lesson.

From that evening Toad was a changed animal, quieter, kinder and wiser than before. Whenever he felt the old craze rising in him, he thought of the dungeon, the barge and his good friends, and the feeling passed.

The Wild Wooders never forgot the night when four animals burst up through the floor of Toad Hall. After that they treated Badger and his friends with great respect, and weasel mothers warned their naughty children that Badger would come.

Mole and Rat went back to their quiet days of boating, picnics and long talks by the fire, and Badger visited them often. The river rolled on under the willows, and the four friends were happy for many, many years.

Toad talked of dusty roads, white villages, sleepy towns and the glorious freedom of the open sky until the whole stable yard seemed to ring with his eloquence. Rat, who wanted nothing in the world but his river, folded his arms and refused, yet he could not help noticing the eager shine in Mole's eyes. At last, with a sigh of resignation, he agreed to come along, rather than leave his friend to the mercy of Toad's enthusiasm, and it was settled that they would start the next morning.

Early the next morning Toad bustled about the yard, shouting orders that nobody needed, while Rat and Mole quietly packed food, blankets and saucepans into the lockers. The cream-coloured horse, who looked far from pleased with the adventure, was harnessed at last, and the little yellow house lurched out of the gate. Toad's servants waved from the steps, and Toad waved back as though he were setting out to conquer a continent.

All through the golden morning the caravan creaked and rattled along quiet lanes between tall hedges, and the white dust rose in little clouds behind the wheels. Toad strode beside the horse's head, composing a song in his own honour, while Rat and Mole sat on the steps and breathed in the sweet smell of hay and honeysuckle. Cottages and orchards slipped by, and Mole, to whom everything was new, felt that he had never been so completely content.

At noon they halted beneath a spreading chestnut tree to eat their cold luncheon and let the horse graze. Toad filled the air with grand schemes, naming towns he meant to visit and sights he meant to see, though it soon became clear that he had no idea where the road would lead. Rat nodded politely and said nothing, but Mole noticed the twinkle in his eye.

At dusk they drew up on a quiet common, where the horse was unharnessed and left to graze among the rushes. Over a simple supper the three friends sat on the caravan steps and watched the stars appear one by one, while Toad, filled with food and glory, talked of the adventures that surely lay ahead. Mole listened, drowsy and happy, and Rat sat silent, content simply to have his friends beside him.

The next morning Toad lay snoring in his bunk, so Rat and Mole, grumbling a little, fed the horse, fetched water from a spring, lit the fire and cooked a breakfast of bacon and tea. When Toad finally strolled out, yawning and stretching, he praised the loveliness of the morning at great length and said nothing whatever about the work that had been done. Mole could not help smiling, while Rat folded his arms and looked at the sky with a patient expression.

They were ambling along the white road one sleepy afternoon when a faint “Poop-poop” sounded far behind them, like the warning of some distant animal. A cloud of dust rolled closer and closer, and a moment later a huge motor car roared past, a glittering vision of plate glass and shining paint that was gone before anyone could say a word. The sound of its horn died away, but the dust it had stirred hung in the air like smoke.

The poor cream-coloured horse reared up in terror, plunged sideways across the road and dragged the caravan into the ditch, where it fell over with a crash of splintering wood and breaking crockery. Rat, jumping up and down in the road, shook his fist at the vanished car and cried out that its driver was a villain, a scoundrel and a road hog who should be reported at once. Mole, trying to calm the trembling horse, could only stare at the wreck of Toad's bright and shining dream.

Toad, far from being angry, sat down in the dust of the road with his legs stretched out and gazed after the vanished car with a rapt and shining face. “The poetry of motion,” he murmured, “the real way to travel, the only way,” and he went on to speak of villages skipped and towns jumped, always somebody else's horizon. Every few moments he sighed “Poop-poop” in a trembling voice, like an animal in a trance.

Rat seized Toad by the shoulders and shook him, begging him to come to his senses and help to drag the poor caravan out of the ditch. Toad merely smiled in a dreamy fashion and declared that the caravan was a worthless toy, a mere stage on his journey to something infinitely grander. From this moment, he announced, his whole life would be given to motor cars, and nothing his friends could say would turn him from it.

At last Rat and Mole coaxed the dreaming Toad to his feet, led the horse by the bridle and walked to the nearest town, where an innkeeper promised to fetch the broken caravan. They left Toad at a table with a heap of luncheon in front of him and the faraway look still in his eyes, and returned home by the evening train. As they travelled, Rat predicted gloomily that Toad's newest craze would be the worst, and not even Mole's cheerful nature could quite persuade him otherwise.

Every morning, while mist still hung over the water, Rat took his pupil out in the little boat and showed him how to hold the oars and how to pull with his back instead of his arms. Mole's paws were blistered and his dignity bruised, yet he was determined not to be beaten by two lengths of wood. By the end of the first week he could steer a straight line, and Rat declared himself astonished and proud.

On the hottest afternoons Rat led his friend into the shallows and taught him to swim, supporting him gently at first and then letting him struggle alone. Mole splashed and spluttered and swallowed a surprising quantity of the river, yet before the summer was over he could float on his back and kick across a pool with something very like grace. Rat watched from the bank with the air of a proud teacher whose lessons had finally taken root.

Day by day Rat revealed the secrets of the river, pointing out the kingfisher that flashed like a blue jewel, the moorhens that bustled among the reeds and the fat, silent fish that hung in the shady pools. Mole learned the names of the water plants, the smell of the mud after rain and the way the current ran faster round a bend. He had been a creature of the dark earth, but he was fast becoming a creature of the light and the stream.

One golden evening, when the sun was sinking behind the willows, Rat sat on the bank with a stub of pencil, watching a family of ducks dabble busily in the shallows. He had begun a little song about them, with a rhythm like the splash of their paddling feet, and he hummed it over and over, frowning at each line. Mole listened with deep admiration, for it had never occurred to him that anyone could make music out of a duck.

Otter often called on his friends in the evening and sat on the bank with his feet in the water, telling long and funny stories of the river and its inhabitants. He spoke with great pride of his small son Portly, who was just learning to swim and was already a menace to every duck and frog in the neighbourhood. Mole laughed until he cried, and little thought that the same small Portly would one day cause them a night of terror.

The long summer days slid by like beads on a string, each one warmer and lazier than the last, until the farmers cut the hay and the corn stood tall and golden in the fields. In the evenings Mole and Rat strolled among the sheaves, watching the last harvest carts rumble home under a sky the colour of apricots. Mole had never imagined that a life so quiet could be so full, and he wished the season might last for ever.

Then autumn crept in, and the willows let fall their yellow leaves, which floated down the river like a fleet of tiny golden boats. The hedges were heavy with berries, the mornings were sharp with mist, and the evenings drew in earlier every day. Rat, who had loved the summer with all his heart, began to look a little drowsy and thoughtful, as if the river itself were preparing for sleep.

When the first hard frosts stiffened the reeds, many of the river folk retired to their holes for the winter, and Rat himself began to nod by the fire for hours at a time. Mole, who was wide awake and full of curiosity, wandered about the house and the bank, and now and then he felt a little lonely. The river, once so busy, had become a grey road of cold, slow water.

Soon the snow came, falling softly through a leaden sky until the river bank lay muffled and silent beneath a thick white blanket. Mole stood at the window of Rat's cosy room and stared across the fields to where the dark line of the Wild Wood showed through the whiteness like a stain. The thought of what might live there, and of the old Badger he had never met, had begun to haunt him.

At last Mole could bear it no longer, and he asked whether they might not call on Badger, who lived so near and seemed such an interesting character. Rat looked up sleepily and shook his head, explaining that Badger could not be hurried or visited like an ordinary neighbour, and that anyone who wished to know him must wait until he chose to come. It was gentle advice, but it only made Mole more curious than ever, and that night he lay awake dreaming of a strange, shy animal in the heart of the wood.

One bitter afternoon Rat fell fast asleep in his armchair, a half-finished poem lying forgotten on his knee. Mole watched the embers sink for a long while, listening to the clock and feeling the whole house hush around him, until a restless boldness began to stir in his chest. If Badger would not be called upon, he thought, then surely Badger might be surprised.

Mole buttoned his coat, took a stout stick and crept out of the door on tiptoe, leaving his friend still snoring gently in the firelight. The afternoon was cold and grey, and the frozen fields crackled underfoot as he set off in a straight line for the dark edge of the Wild Wood. At first the adventure felt delightful, for he had never before gone anywhere entirely alone.

At length he reached the edge of the Wild Wood, where the bare trees crowded together, black against the whitening sky, and the undergrowth lay tangled with snow. Mole stepped between the first trunks with a rather bold air, for nothing yet seemed to threaten him, but the light grew dimmer at every step and the silence seemed to listen to him. Dead leaves, fallen branches and hollow trunks lay all about, and it came to him that this was a place without a single friendly corner.

Suddenly Mole saw a small, wedge-shaped face with hard, bright eyes watching him from a hole among the roots, and then it was gone as swiftly as it had come. He told himself that he had imagined it, but a moment later another face appeared, and another, until it seemed that every hole in the wood was full of watchers. Mole walked on faster, trying to look as though he noticed nothing, yet his heart was beating hard.

Then, from somewhere behind him, came a thin, shrill whistle, and from far ahead another whistle answered it, as though the whole wood were passing along a message. After that there came a soft pattering, like the sound of rain on dead leaves, which grew louder and nearer and seemed to come at him from every direction at once. Mole stopped dead in the snow, listened with every nerve in his body and felt the first cold touch of real fear.

Terror seized him at last, and Mole ran blindly, dodging between the trunks, while the thin whistling rose behind him and the pattering seemed to close in on every side. Twigs lashed his face, brambles tore at his coat, and roots reached up out of the snow to catch his feet, so that the whole wood appeared to be hunting him. Dimly he understood that he had made a terrible mistake, and that the afternoon was fading into the dusk of a winter evening.

At last he saw a dark hollow at the foot of a great old beech, and he flung himself into it, burrowing among the dry leaves and the crumbling wood until he was entirely hidden. There he lay, panting and shaking, while the footsteps pattered round the tree and the whistles rose and fell outside like the voices of invisible hunters. He was a long way from the warm fireside, and he began bitterly to wish that he had listened to Rat.

Back in the warm house, Rat woke from his doze with a start, called out for his friend and found nothing but an empty room and a dying fire. A glance at the door showed him small footprints leading away across the snow, straight towards the Wild Wood, and Rat understood at once what had happened. Without wasting a moment, he buckled on a belt, thrust a pair of pistols into it, seized his stoutest stick and set off after Mole as fast as he could go.

Rat followed the footprints into the Wild Wood with a calm and steady step, whistling quietly as he went, as though he were strolling down a village lane. From their holes and hollows the hidden watchers glared at him, but when they saw the pistols in his belt and the grim set of his jaw, they drew back and made no sound at all. Every now and then he called out Mole's name in a clear voice that rang between the trees.

At last Rat's voice came ringing through the trees, and a moment later his face appeared at the mouth of the hollow, calm and kindly and quite unafraid. Mole poured out his apologies in a flood, confessing that he had been a fool and that he would never doubt his friend's advice again. Rat only patted his shoulder, told him that nearly every animal feels the terror of the Wild Wood once, and promised that they would soon be safe.

Before they had gone far, great soft flakes began to whirl through the branches, and within minutes the ground, the roots and the paths had vanished beneath a smooth white blanket. Rat stopped, looked all around with a worried frown and admitted that every landmark he knew had been rubbed out by the storm. Night was coming on, the cold was deepening, and the two friends were lost in the very place where nobody wished to be lost.

On they trudged, floundering through drifts that rose above their knees, but every tree looked exactly like the last, and the circle of snow around them seemed to follow them wherever they went. Mole, who had begun the day as a bold adventurer, was now so exhausted that he could hardly lift his feet, and Rat had to coax him forward with cheerful words he did not entirely feel. The wood was silent except for the creak of branches under their white burden.

Suddenly Mole caught his foot on something hard beneath the snow and pitched forward on his face, crying out that he had cut his shin on a piece of buried iron. Rat hurried to him, examined the leg with a practised eye, and then, instead of offering comfort, began to scratch and scrape at the snow with a look of rising excitement. Mole sat up and stared, quite certain that his friend had lost his wits in the cold.

“Mole, you are a wonder,” said Rat joyfully, for the object that had cut his shin was no scrap of rubbish but an honest scraper, the kind that stands beside a door for wiping boots. Where there was a scraper there must be a mat, he argued, and where there was a mat there must be a house, so the two friends dug until their paws were numb. At last the snow fell away from a solid green door set into a bank, with a bell-pull hanging beside it and a brass plate beneath.

The brass plate bore the words Mr Badger in neat capital letters, and Rat, with a whoop of delight, seized the bell-pull and gave it a long and vigorous tug. Far, far inside the hill, a deep and distant clanging rang out, and the friends stood shivering on the step while the snow settled on their shoulders. For a long moment nothing happened, and then they heard the slow shuffle of slippers coming nearer.

The door opened a crack, and a long snout and a pair of sleepy, blinking eyes appeared in the opening, while a gruff voice growled that the next time this happened, its owner would be exceedingly angry. Rat stepped forward and cried out that it was only Rat and Mole, lost in the snow, and the growl changed at once to a cry of welcome. Badger, in an old dressing gown and a pair of worn slippers, flung the door wide and pulled them inside.

Badger took a lamp and led them down a long, low passage and into a spacious kitchen with a floor of worn red brick and a great open hearth. Hams, bundles of dried herbs, nets of onions and baskets of eggs hung from the beams of the ceiling, and a cheerful fire blazed in the fireplace, throwing a ruddy light across the dresser and the long table. Rat and Mole sank onto the benches, and for the first time that day they felt warm and safe.

Rat explained how they had come to be wandering in the Wild Wood on such a night, and Mole sat by the fire, staring at his feet with burning cheeks. Badger listened with his paws behind his back and a grave expression, and when the tale was told he said that he would not scold anybody, for a stormy evening was no time for lectures. He merely added, with a shake of his head, that anyone who visited the Wild Wood in winter must expect to meet something unpleasant.

Badger bustled about the kitchen, laying the table with plates, knives and a great jug, and he brought out cold meat, pickles, fresh bread and a large piece of cheese. The two travellers fell upon the food as though they had not eaten for a week, and Rat, between mouthfuls, praised every dish with sincere enthusiasm. Slowly the terrors of the afternoon faded, and the Wild Wood seemed a mere bad dream that belonged to another world.

When the plates were cleared, Badger stirred the fire and asked for news of the river bank, and Rat told him how Toad had bought a motor car and was wrecking it again and again. Badger listened with a frown that grew darker every moment, and at last he said that matters could not be left as they were, though nothing could be done until the winter was over. His voice was gruff, but Mole could hear that he cared a great deal about the foolish Toad.

The next morning, when Rat and Mole came yawning into the kitchen, they found two young hedgehogs sitting at the table, eating porridge with great concentration. The little visitors scrambled to their feet and bowed shyly, for they had been lost in the snow the day before, on their way to school, and Badger had taken them in for the night. Their porridge was nearly gone, but their eyes were still round with wonder at the grand company that had come down to breakfast.

After breakfast Badger settled himself by the fire and told them a strange story that his own grandfathers had handed down. Long ago, he said, there had stood a great city of people on the very ground where the Wild Wood now grew, and its streets and houses had been busy and proud and full of life. They had built well, he added, as though they meant to stay for ever.

In time the people went away, the walls crumbled in rain and frost, and the forest crept slowly over every stone until nothing remained but green hills and tangled roots. The animals, who are always the last to be remembered and the first to find a roof, moved into the ruins and made homes in the halls and passages beneath. Badger, speaking quietly, said that his own ancestors had been among them, and that this was why he loved the place so deeply.

Badger, who clearly enjoyed an admirer, led Mole through his house, past arched doorways and vaulted chambers, down corridors that branched in every direction and into store rooms piled with apples, nuts, turnips and jars of honey. Mole, who had spent his whole life in burrows, gazed up at the great curved ceilings with growing delight and said that he had never known an underground home so spacious or so well planned. Badger, pleased and a little embarrassed, replied gruffly that a good house is only a matter of patience and common sense.

Mole explained, with the eloquence of an expert, that nothing could compare with a home below the ground, where no storm could find you and no frost could creep through the walls. Badger, who had held the same opinion all his life, beamed with satisfaction and declared that a mole after his own heart was a rare and welcome visitor. In that moment a friendship was quietly sealed that would last for the rest of their lives.

When it was time to leave, Badger announced that he knew a short cut to the edge of the wood, one that ran deep beneath the roots where no weasel or stoat could trouble them. He took up a lantern and led his guests into a long, narrow tunnel, so smoothly built that a traveller might have walked it blindfold. The lamplight shone on arching walls and dripping stones, and the three animals, with Badger in front, passed along like a small procession.

As they walked, Badger told them that the Wild Wooders were a mixed lot, some good and some bad, but that all of them knew better than to meddle with him. Then, with a gruffness that did not hide his kindness, he repeated that Toad was a danger to himself and everyone else, and that he would take him in hand as soon as the winter was over. Rat nodded eagerly, and Mole, who had so far seen Toad only at his best, felt a flicker of pity for him.

At last the tunnel climbed and ended in a low opening hidden behind a thicket of brambles, and Rat and Mole crept out, blinking, into the dazzling light of a winter morning. Beyond them the fields lay smooth and white, and the dreaded Wild Wood stood behind them like a sleeping giant that had nothing more to say. Badger shook their paws solemnly, told them to come again whenever they liked, and vanished back into his darkness.

The two friends set off across the glittering fields, their footprints making a long dark line behind them, and the frosty air made their whiskers stiff. Mole said little, for his mind was full of the wonders of the last day, the frightening and the kind, and he knew that he had learned more about the world than in all his months of safe quiet. Rat glanced at him sideways, smiled quietly to himself and said nothing at all, for he knew that some thoughts are best left to grow in peace.

Back in Rat's snug house, Mole ate a hearty supper and stretched his toes toward the fire, feeling as safe as he had ever felt in his life. Yet in the quiet moments between Rat's yawns, his thoughts kept drifting, quite against his will, to the shabby little burrow he had abandoned on that first morning of spring. He had not once looked back until now, and he could not tell why the memory should come to him tonight.

The winter weeks slipped by, grey and white and quiet, and Rat spent most of his days dozing in front of the fire with a book open on his chest. Mole wrapped himself in a long scarf and took long walks along the frozen bank, watching his breath hang in the air, and the memory of his old home came back to him more and more often. It had not been much of a house, he told himself, but it had been entirely his own.

One crisp afternoon Rat declared that they were both growing lazy and ought to take a proper country walk, and he set off briskly across the frozen fields with Mole trotting at his side. They talked and laughed as they went, stopping now and then to look at a frosted spider's web or a robin hopping on a fence, while the pale sun sank lower and lower behind the hills. By the time they turned for home the sky had begun to darken to a deep, cold blue.

As dusk gathered they came to a sleepy village, where a yellow light glowed behind every curtain and smoke rose in thin lines from the chimneys. Mole slowed down to look at the cosy rooms as they passed, glimpsing a family at supper here, a cat on a windowsill there, and each little scene reminded him how much he loved a home.
