Rat strode on ahead, humming happily, and did not notice that his friend had begun to drag behind.

Beyond the village they turned into a frosty lane, where the hedges stood stiff and silver in the starlight, and suddenly Mole stopped dead in the middle of the road. Out of the cold air had drifted a tiny, familiar whiff, so faint that anyone else would have missed it entirely, but to Mole it was as clear as the ringing of a bell. He lifted his nose, trembling all over, and tried with every nerve in his body to catch that precious whiff again.

It was the smell of his own old home, the shabby little house he had abandoned in the first rush of spring, and it called to him through the darkness as plainly as if somebody were speaking his name. All at once he remembered the whitewash, the low ceiling, the plaster figures in the garden and the friendly quiet of his own front room, and the memories came rushing back like a wave. A great sob rose in his chest, and before he could stop it, tears were running down his cheeks.

Rat, who was striding on ahead, was slow to notice that his companion had fallen behind, and when he turned back at last he found Mole standing helpless in the road, shaking with sobs. Rat hurried to his side and asked gently what could be wrong, and Mole, between gasps, tried to explain that it was only a smell, a silly little smell, and that he could not bear it. Rat said nothing, but he put an arm round his friend's shoulders and waited until the worst was over.

At last Mole managed to explain that it was the smell of his old home, a poor little place that he had hardly thought of for months, and that it seemed to be calling him back. He knew it was shabby and dusty, he said, and he knew that Rat's house was a thousand times finer, yet nothing in the world could stop him longing for the one thing that was truly his own. Rat listened quietly and understood completely, and he was not in the least offended by this praise of another house.

Rat declared at once that the matter must be settled there and then, and that they would search for the old home even if it took them until morning. He told Mole to go where his nose led, promising that he would follow and keep him company wherever the trail ran. Mole, wiping his eyes, lifted his nose into the wind and set off with a small, shaky hope kindling inside him.

Step by step Mole followed the thread of scent, turning down a narrow path, crossing a frozen ditch and scrambling over a low bank, while Rat followed patiently with a hand on his shoulder. The faint smell grew stronger until it was a clear and certain invitation, and at last Mole stopped beside a heap of dead leaves and a patch of trampled snow and whispered that this was the very place. Rat knelt down and began to scrabble at the leaves, and behind them a dark opening appeared in the bank.

They crawled down a narrow tunnel into the darkness, Mole leading the way, until his paws touched a small front door, and there above it, in cheap white letters, was the name he had chosen long ago. Mole End, it said, and as he read it, the tears came again, though this time they were mixed with a trembling smile. He took a deep breath, turned the handle and went in with Rat close behind him.

Inside, Mole End was cold and dark and silent, and thick dust lay over every chair, shelf and picture, while cobwebs hung in the corners like grey curtains. Mole stood in the doorway, holding his breath, as though the house might wake and reproach him for having left it alone so long. He felt ashamed that his best friend should see his poor home in such a state.

Rat found a lamp on the hall table and lit it, and the little house glowed softly into being, with its neat rooms, its low ceilings and its row of pictures. The small plaster statues still stood on their shelves, smiling blindly into the dust, and everything was exactly where Mole had left it on that morning of spring. The whole place seemed to hold its breath, waiting to see what its owner would say.

Mole sank into a chair, buried his face in his paws and wept, declaring that he should never have brought Rat to such a dreary place on such a bitter night. There was no fire, no supper and no welcome, he sobbed, and he had dragged his friend a long way from a warm house for nothing. It seemed to him that he had spoiled the best evening of the winter.

Rat only laughed and told him not to be silly, and then, without another word, he went briskly from room to room, lighting lamps, shaking out dust sheets and raking the cold ashes in the grate. Within minutes a small fire was crackling merrily, and the chilly little parlour had begun to look almost welcoming. Mole watched him through his tears and slowly stopped crying, struck by the plain, steady goodness of his friend.

Rat rummaged through every cupboard, tapping tins and sniffing jars, and at last he announced in triumph that he had found a box of biscuits, a tin of sardines and a sausage in silver paper. Mole protested that it was a poor supper for a guest, but Rat insisted that two hungry travellers could ask for nothing finer. Together they began to lay the table, and Mole, in spite of himself, felt a small glow of pleasure.

Just then they heard a shuffling of many small feet outside the door, followed by whispers, coughs and the rustle of paper, as though a crowd of shy visitors were preparing for a performance. A sharp little voice counted “one, two, three,” and then, out of the darkness of the passage, a thin and tuneful choir began to sing. Mole raised his head and listened intently, his tears quite forgotten, wondering who could possibly be abroad on such a night.

Rat flung open the door, and there, in the light of a dozen swinging lanterns, stood a ring of little field mice with red woollen scarves wound round their throats and their paws tucked into their sleeves for warmth. Their breath rose in white puffs as they sang a carol of the frosty season, about villagers gathering and bells ringing across the snow, and their thin, sweet voices filled the narrow passage. Mole stood motionless in the doorway, hardly daring to breathe, afraid that the beautiful moment might vanish if he moved.

Mole begged the singers to come in out of the cold, and they crowded round the fire, stamping their feet and warming their paws on mugs of hot spiced ale that Rat had heated on the stove. Rat took a handful of coins from his pocket, pressed them into the paw of the eldest mouse and asked him to hurry to the village shop and bring back the best supper that money could buy. The little fellow saluted, gathered a friend or two and was off through the tunnel like a streak of grey.

Before long the eldest mouse came pattering back with a basket piled high with good things, and the little table in Mole's parlour disappeared beneath a feast that nobody would have believed possible an hour earlier. They ate and laughed and passed the dishes from paw to paw, and the field mice, bright-eyed and chattering, told stories of their lives in the cornfields. Mole, presiding at the head of his own table, felt for the first time in months like a proper host in a proper home.

When the last of the singers had said goodnight and gone off along the passage, Mole climbed into his own old bed, pulled the quilt up to his chin and gazed contentedly at the low ceiling. In the next bed Rat was already asleep, smiling a little, and the dying fire cast a rosy glow over the shabby furniture that he had once been so ashamed of. Mole understood at last that he could love the river and his old home together, and that having both made him the richest animal in the world.

All through the winter bad news came from Toad Hall: he had bought several motor cars, smashed each in turn, been carried to hospital three times and paid enormous fines. At last, on a bright morning in the new year, Badger himself appeared at Rat's door, grave and determined and wearing a stout old coat. He announced that Toad's folly had gone far enough, and that the three of them must go to Toad Hall that very day and take the culprit in hand.

At Toad Hall they found a huge new motor car shining before the door, and down the steps strutted Toad in goggles, gauntlets and an enormous overcoat, inviting them to come for a splendid spin. Badger looked at him without a trace of a smile, took one of his arms while Rat took the other, and together they marched the kicking and protesting Toad into the house. Inside, they stripped off his motoring clothes, and Badger ordered the servants to put the car away and never to bring it out again.

Badger lectured him for a long time on his foolishness, his danger and the grief that he was causing his friends, and Toad wept, sniffed and nodded in all the right places until even Mole began to soften. But when Badger asked him to promise that he would never touch a motor car again, Toad's face changed, and he announced boldly that he would promise nothing of the sort. He was not sorry in the least, he said, and the poetry of motion was worth all the fines in the world.

Badger declared that there was only one remedy: Toad must be locked in his own bedroom until he had come to his senses. The three friends moved into Toad Hall to keep watch, and they took turns to sit by his door, day and night, so that there could be no escape and no mischief. Toad stormed and sulked and begged through the keyhole, but nobody would give way, and the long days crept by.

When it was Rat's turn to keep watch, Toad let out a long and horrible groan and told him, in a voice that faded to a whisper, that he was dying and had only a few hours left. Rat, who was soft-hearted but not stupid, suspected a trick, yet he could not take the risk of being wrong, so he locked the door behind him and hurried away to fetch a doctor. That was exactly what the cunning Toad had been hoping for ever since the key had turned in the lock.

The instant Rat's footsteps had died away, Toad leapt from his bed, tied his sheets and blankets into a long rope, fastened one end to the window and slid down the wall to the garden below. He crept past the stables on tiptoe, scrambled over the fence and then set off across the fields at a run, laughing aloud at his own cleverness. Nothing in the world, he told himself, could stop a Toad of his talents.

Toad strolled for miles until he came to a roadside inn called the Red Lion, where he ordered a large and expensive lunch and ate it with the satisfaction of a free and conquering animal. As he was paying his bill, he glanced out of the window into the inn yard and saw a handsome motor car standing there, its owners nowhere in sight. His heart began to thump with longing, and every sensible thought he had ever had flew straight out of his head.

Toad told himself that he would only look at the car, and then that he would only sit in the driver's seat, and then that he would only turn the handle to see what would happen. Before he knew it, the engine was purring and he was racing down the lane at a most illegal speed, singing at the top of his voice and feeling like a king. The wind roared in his ears, the hedges blurred into one green stripe, and he did not spare a single thought for his friends, the law or the consequences.

Toad tore through one village after another, scattering hens, frightening carthorses and causing a farmer to shake his fist so hard that his hat fell off. Before long a pair of police constables had joined the pursuit, and when at last the stolen car coughed and stopped beside a ditch, they dragged the astonished driver out by the scruff of his coat. Toad, who had been dreaming of cheering crowds and glory, found himself led away in handcuffs and quite unable to think of a single clever word.

In the crowded courtroom, an old judge with a face like stone listed Toad's crimes one by one: the theft of a motor car, furious and dangerous driving, and a quite shocking amount of cheek to the police. A clerk added up the proper penalties and announced that they came to nineteen years, whereupon the judge, with a grim nod, remarked that it might as well be a round twenty. Toad was led out of the court in a daze, and a heavy door clanged behind the wealthiest and proudest animal on the river bank.

One hot evening in midsummer, Otter appeared at Rat's door, pale and breathless, with the look of an animal who has run a very long way. His small son Portly, he said, had slipped away from home before dawn and had not been seen since, and although Otter had searched every hole and reed bed for miles, he had found no trace of him. His voice shook when he mentioned the weir, where the water ran deep and dangerous.

Otter declared that he would keep watch at the shallow ford where Portly had first learned to swim, because it was the place the youngster loved best, and he would not stir until his son was found. Rat took his friend's paw in both of his and promised to search every stretch of the river, and Mole, without being asked, ran to launch the boat. They set off in the cool evening, determined not to come back without good news.

Rat pulled steadily at the oars while Mole sat in the bow, and the little boat slid upstream through the failing light, past sleeping meadows and silent reed beds. Every few minutes they called Portly's name along the banks and peered into every hole and hollow, but the only answer was the ripple of the water and the distant call of an owl. Neither of them thought of turning back, though the night was growing darker with every stroke.

Presently the moon rose, large and round and silver, and it laid a path of light across the water that guided them on like a lamp. The meadows lay pale and still, the willows were black shapes against the sky, and a strange hush seemed to settle over the world, as if the night were waiting for something to happen. Mole shivered, though the summer air was warm, and Rat rowed on in a silence that neither of them wished to break.

Suddenly Rat let the oars drift and raised his head, with an expression of rapt wonder on his face, as though he were listening to something far beyond the range of ordinary ears. “Do you hear it,” he whispered, “that tune, that wonderful, piping tune, calling and calling and never quite finishing?” Mole listened as hard as he could, but he heard only the wind in the reeds and the soft lap of the stream.

Rat turned the boat toward the music like a sleepwalker, and Mole, who could hear nothing, followed his friend's lead and trusted him completely. The air grew heavy with the scent of meadowsweet and wild roses, and the colours of the banks seemed richer and stranger than they had ever been by daylight. Little by little the stars paled, and a faint grey light began to creep into the east.

Before long they heard the low, steady roar of a weir, and out of the dawn mist rose a little island, green and wooded, lying in a quiet loop of the stream. They tied the boat to a willow root, stepped ashore on grass that sparkled with dew and pushed their way through a thicket of wild apple, hawthorn and honeysuckle. Everything about the place was so lovely and so strangely hushed that they stood spellbound at the edge of the trees.

In a green clearing at the heart of the island, Mole felt a great and gentle presence close at hand, and he began to tremble from head to foot, though no cold wind was blowing. Rat, kneeling beside him with his head bowed, whispered that he was afraid and yet not afraid, because the power that filled the place seemed to wish them nothing but good. Neither of them dared to raise their eyes, and yet each of them knew that they were about to see something that few creatures had ever seen.

They raised their eyes and saw him: Pan, the great god of wild things, with curved horns and kind, laughing eyes, the pipes still raised in his hand as though the last note had only just died away. Between his hooves, curled up as peacefully as a child in a cradle, lay little Portly, fast asleep and perfectly safe. Rat and Mole felt a joy so large that it could hardly be borne, and they sank to the ground and bowed their heads.

As the sun rose and the first birds began to sing, the vision faded, and on the breeze came a gentle gift, the gift of forgetfulness, so that the wonder should not weigh upon their ordinary lives. Rat and Mole lifted the sleeping Portly into the boat and rowed home along the shining river, and when they reached the shallow ford, Otter ran into the water to snatch up his son, weeping for joy. Only a faint, sweet echo of music lingered in their minds, and neither could say where they had heard it.

Toad was taken to the strongest prison in the land, a grim ancient castle with walls many feet thick, rusty chains hanging in the corridors and a guard at every turning. He was led down flight after flight of worn steps, past one heavy door after another, until a jailer thrust him into a dark cell and locked it with a hollow clang. Far above him, in the sunshine, the world went on without a thought for its most famous driver.

Toad flung himself on the cold stone floor and wept until he had no tears left, thinking of his beautiful house, his lawns and his boathouse, and of the friends he had treated so badly. Twenty years was such an enormous length of time that he would be an old, bent creature before he saw the sunshine again, and all the motor cars in the world would be forgotten. For the first time in his life he saw that his own foolishness had brought him to this.

The jailer had a daughter, a gentle, kind-hearted girl who was fond of animals of every kind, and she could not bear to hear the poor prisoner sobbing night after night. One evening she crept down to his cell with a tray of strong hot tea and a pile of buttered toast, and the smell of it was so delicious that Toad lifted his head for the first time in days. He drank and ate gratefully, and a little of his old spirit began to return.

The girl sat down on a stool and asked him gently to tell her about the grand house that she had heard him sobbing over, and Toad, delighted to find an audience at last, began to boast again. He described the lawns, the boathouse, the fishponds, the banqueting hall and the long line of servants who had bowed when he walked by, and she listened with wide and admiring eyes. By the time he had finished, he felt almost like his old self again, and the cold walls of the dungeon no longer seemed quite so cruel.

Then, lowering her voice, the girl told him that she was fond of animals and could not bear to see a creature so unhappy. Her aunt, she explained, was the washerwoman who came to the prison every week to collect the dirty linen, and a thought had come to her that a clever prisoner might put to use. Toad, who had never before been called clever by a jailer's daughter, pricked up his ears at once.

When she explained the plan, Toad drew himself up in horror, for the great Toad of Toad Hall was far too grand to be seen in a washerwoman's gown. Then he remembered the damp walls, the twenty long years and the girl's calm and friendly face, and his pride slowly gave way to common sense. He said, with great dignity, that he would consider her proposal, and by the next morning he had accepted it.

On Monday the old washerwoman arrived with her big basket, and the jailer's daughter led her into the cell, where a brisk bargain was quickly made. Toad handed over every coin in his purse, and in return the good woman, who was glad of the money, agreed to give up her gown, her apron, her shawl and her bonnet. She promised to wait quietly in the cell, as though Toad had overpowered her, until he was safely away.

The jailer's daughter helped him into the long cotton gown, tied the strings of the apron behind him, pinned the shawl over his shoulders and settled the bonnet carefully on his head. Toad turned this way and that in the dim light and saw, to his surprise and secret delight, that he made a most convincing washerwoman, round and stout and entirely respectable. She gave him the washerwoman's basket and told him exactly which way to walk.

With his heart thumping inside his borrowed gown, Toad walked along the dark corridors, climbed the stairs and passed through door after door, and each guard he met touched his cap and wished the old lady a good night. One of them made a joke about the washing that was dreadfully rude, and Toad, who had never been spoken to like that in his life, had to bite his tongue to keep from replying in his proper voice. At last the great gate swung open, and he stepped out through it into the cool night air.

Outside the gate, Toad drew a deep breath of the cool night air and was very nearly tempted to dance for joy, which would have ruined everything. Instead he forced himself to walk sedately down the hill toward the twinkling lights of the town, swinging his basket like an honest woman going home. He was free, and the thought of his comfortable home was so sweet that it almost made him cry.

At the railway station a long train stood puffing and hissing beside the platform, and Toad, with a swelling heart, fumbled in the pockets of his gown for the fare. To his dismay he found nothing there, for he had given every coin to the old washerwoman, and he stood helpless in the lamplight, wondering how a toad of his talents could be defeated by a ticket. Then he noticed the engine driver, leaning from his cab with an oil can in his paw.

Toad put on his most pitiful voice and told the engine driver a mournful tale of a poor washerwoman who had lost her money and could not get home to her children. The driver, who was a good-natured man, promised her a free ride on his engine if she would only wash a few of his shirts when she arrived. Toad accepted the bargain at once, privately resolving to do nothing of the kind.

Soon the train was thundering through the dark countryside, trailing sparks and smoke, and Toad stood on the footplate with his bonnet blown crooked, laughing at the wind and the speed and the glory of it all. He was so happy that he forgot to be careful, and he began to tell the driver a boastful story of how he had escaped from prison, and how clever he had been. The driver listened in silence, his eyes fixed on the track ahead and his face growing graver with every word.

Just then the driver glanced back along the line and saw another engine racing after them, its fire glowing red in the darkness and a crowd of policemen waving from its cab. He turned to Toad with a stern face and said that he had been told a pretty story, but that the washerwoman had turned out to be a convict, and that this was an awkward business for an honest driver. Then the corners of his mouth twitched, and he added that he had never much cared for policemen, and that he would see the matter through.

Toad seized a shovel and heaped coal into the glowing furnace with such energy that the engine roared faster and faster through the night, rocking from side to side and trailing a tail of fire. The police engine fell back a little, but it never gave up, and its whistle screamed behind them in the darkness like an angry animal. Sparks flew, the rails sang, and Toad, red-faced and blackened with soot, thought it the finest moment of his life.

Ahead of them, at the foot of a hill, lay the black mouth of a long tunnel, and the driver, shouting above the din, told Toad exactly what he must do. As soon as they came out at the far end, he would slow the engine, and Toad must leap down and hide among the trees beside the line before the police engine emerged. It was a desperate plan, but Toad could think of nothing better, and he nodded and gripped the rail.

As the engine slowed, Toad let go of the rail, jumped into the dark and rolled over and over down the bank, to lie panting in the long wet grass with his bonnet tilted over one eye. A moment later the police engine thundered past, so close that the sparks fell around him, and its crew, who were gazing eagerly ahead, never thought to look back. Toad waited until the last red light had vanished, and then, shaking with relief and laughter, he crept away into the wood.

It was a long and chilly night in the wood, full of rustlings, creaks and the cries of owls, and Toad, who had never in his life slept anywhere but in a feather bed, found it a most unfriendly place. At last he discovered a hollow tree, curled himself up in the dry leaves at the bottom of it and wrapped his shawl tightly round his shoulders. He fell asleep dreaming of Toad Hall, its warm rooms and its sumptuous breakfasts.

He woke at dawn, stiff, hungry and covered with leaves, and wandered through the wood until he came to a canal, where a patient horse was plodding along the towpath, pulling a long, brightly painted barge behind it. A stout woman at the stern, with her sleeves rolled up and a heap of washing at her feet, called out to ask whether the poor old lady would care to come aboard for a bite of breakfast. Toad, who had eaten nothing since the jailer's daughter's tea and who could already smell bacon frying somewhere below, accepted the invitation gladly.

Toad had never washed so much as a handkerchief in his life, and under his clumsy paws the woman's linen turned from white to grey and from grey to a dismal brown, while the soapy water slopped across the deck. She watched with growing amusement and then with growing suspicion, and when she remarked that she had never seen a worse washerwoman in all her days, Toad lost his temper and roared that he was a famous Toad. In an instant she had seen through the disguise, and with a shriek of fury she seized him by the legs and flung him into the canal.

Toad scrambled out of the water, dripping and spluttering and boiling with rage, while the woman on the barge laughed so hard that she could scarcely stand. Then, sweeping off his dripping bonnet, he ran along the towpath, unhooked the horse from its tow rope, scrambled onto its broad back and drove it away at a gallop, with the woman's furious shouts growing fainter behind him. The great horse, who had spent years plodding at a walk, seemed rather to enjoy the change.

After a long gallop Toad came upon a gipsy, sitting on a stool beside a camp fire with a pot of stew bubbling merrily over the flames, and the smell of it nearly made him faint. The gipsy looked the great horse over with a knowing eye, and after a long and shrewd bargain, Toad sold it for six shillings and sixpence and as much hot breakfast as he could eat. He considered it a very fair price, since the horse had cost him nothing.

Toad ate until he could hold no more, thanked his host with a flourish that was almost too grand for a washerwoman and set off again along the white road, warm, well fed and brimming with confidence. The sun was shining, the coins jingled in his pocket, and every hedge he passed seemed to bow to him as the cleverest and most fortunate animal in the whole county. Gone were the dungeon, the chains and the long years of punishment, and Toad could think only of home.

As he walked, Toad went over his escapes one by one, and each time he told the tale to himself it grew a little grander, until he forgot how much help he had received. Before the lane ended he was singing at the top of his voice, in a song of his own making, that no prison could hold so clever a Toad, and that no policeman could catch such a hero. His cleverness, he decided, was a gift that only a handful of animals in history had ever possessed.

Presently he heard behind him a sound that he knew only too well, the faint, wicked, enchanting “Poop-poop” of a motor horn, and a large car came gliding up and slowed down beside him. The kind people inside leaned out to say that they were going a long way and would gladly give a lift to the poor old lady with the bonnet, if she cared for it. Toad felt a strange shiver run through him from his nose to the tips of his toes.

Toad climbed in with great dignity and sat quietly for a time, but the sights, the smells and the noise of the engine worked on him like a spell, and his paws began to twitch on his lap. At last he could bear it no longer: he sprang up, shoved the astonished driver out of his seat, seized the wheel and shouted that he was the great Toad, who could drive better than anyone alive. Before anyone could stop him, he trod hard on the pedal, and the car leapt forward.

The car shot forward faster and faster, swerved across the road, burst through a hedge and, with a tremendous splash, plunged nose first into a deep pond on the other side. Toad was hurled out of his seat, sailed high through the air like a great flapping bird and came down with a thump on the soft grass of the meadow, still wearing most of his bonnet. For a moment he lay there, stunned, and then he sat up and began to laugh until he could laugh no more.

The owners of the car struggled out of the pond, spluttering and shaking their fists, and set off in furious pursuit across the meadow, shouting for the thief to stop. Toad gathered up his skirts, put his head down and ran as he had never run before, leaping ditches, crashing through hedges and scattering a flock of astonished sheep. Behind him the cries grew fainter, but he knew that nothing would save him if he stopped even for a moment.

For many long days after that, Toad lived like a fugitive, hiding by day in ditches and haystacks and creeping along the lanes by night, living on turnips, crusts and whatever he could beg from sleeping farms. His beautiful gown, once so respectable, was torn and muddy, his bonnet had lost its ribbon, and all the pride of those first escapes had dwindled to a single longing for his own comfortable bed. He was dirty, hungry and footsore, but at least he was free, and every night the river drew a little nearer.

One misty morning, from the top of a hill, Toad saw the willows and the silver gleam of the river that he knew so well, and for a long time he stood there with tears running down his dusty face. He had made a fool of himself, he thought, and he had no right to expect any kindness from the friends he had insulted, but Rat's door was the only door in the world that might still open to him. Slowly and wearily, with his ragged skirts trailing behind him, he began to walk down the hill toward the only home that might still welcome him.

Meanwhile, on the river bank, the last of the summer had faded into autumn, and the swallows were gathering in noisy crowds on the roofs and the tall trees, twittering about the long journey that lay ahead. Rat watched them every evening from his doorstep, with a restless, wistful look that Mole had never seen on his face before. He could not have said why they troubled him so, but their chatter seemed to be calling to something deep inside him.

One afternoon Mole asked his friend what was troubling him, and Rat, after a long silence, explained that the swallows were preparing to leave for the warm south, as they did every year. He admitted, a little shyly, that he had begun to wonder what it would be like to follow them, to see the lands they described and to taste the fruit that grew where the sun never failed. Mole was astonished, for he had always supposed that Rat wanted nothing more than his river.

To shake off his restless mood, Rat decided to take a long walk along the high road, which wound away from the river across the fields and over the distant hills. The highway was dusty and silent, and as he followed it, he felt, for the first time in his life, that a river might not be the whole world after all. He walked on slowly, with his paws in his pockets and his thoughts far away.

On the road Rat met a tired, weather-beaten stranger, a lean grey rat with a gold earring, a blue jersey and a faraway look, who wore the dust of a hundred harbours on his boots. He announced, with a polite bow, that he was a Sea Rat, born in the southern ports and sailing from every one of them, and that he was now travelling through the country on business of his own. Rat, delighted at the sight of so interesting a creature, invited him home at once for a meal.

Over a hearty lunch the Sea Rat spoke of his life on the ships, of storms that threw waves higher than a house and of long weeks of calm when there was nothing around him but sky and water. He told of sailing into harbour at dawn with the gulls wheeling overhead, and Rat listened with his chin in his paws, quite forgetting his plate, while Mole, who had never seen the sea, sat wide-eyed. The weathered face of the traveller glowed in the firelight as though it were a lantern in a story.

He described the harbours of the south, where the sea was deep blue and the white towns climbed the hills, where the markets were heaped with oranges and figs, and where fishermen sang at sunset. He spoke of Marseilles, Sicily and Constantinople, and the names rolled off his tongue like music, each one glowing in Rat's mind with a golden light. Rat's paws gripped the arms of his chair, and his food grew cold on the plate while the stranger talked on and on.

The Sea Rat leaned closer, his eyes shining, and said in a low voice that the sea was a great calling thing, and that whoever had once heard it could never be quite at peace on land again. Rat sat very still, his eyes growing dreamy, as if the white sails and the foam and the far blue islands were already rising before him. Mole shifted uneasily in his chair, for he could see that his friend was no longer entirely in the room.

At last the Sea Rat rose to his feet, thanked them for their kindness with the grace of an old campaigner and said that he must be going, for the tide waited for no traveller. Rat followed him to the door and watched in silence as the lean figure with its pack strode away down the road, growing smaller and smaller, until the dust swallowed it. Then he turned back into the room with the stunned look of a creature who has heard far too much.

Rat did not seem to hear Mole's anxious questions, and with a strange, glassy look in his eyes he began to move about the room, stuffing a few belongings, a loaf of bread and his writing things into a satchel. He said, in a flat voice, that he was going south at last, to see the harbours with his own eyes and to feel the sun on the sea, and that Mole could look after the house until he returned. Whether he would ever return, he added in the same dreamy voice, was something that nobody could promise.

Mole planted himself in the doorway, seized his friend firmly by both arms and, with all the quiet strength that he possessed, refused to let him pass. Rat struggled wildly for a moment, glaring at him as if he were a stranger, but the spell was breaking, and at last his strength gave out and he sank to the floor, shaking from head to foot. Mole knelt beside him, holding him close, until the wild light faded from his eyes.

Mole helped his friend into the armchair, poured him a glass of something strengthening and sat beside him, talking quietly about ordinary and comforting things, the river, the fire, the supper they would have. Gradually the shaking stopped, and Rat said, in a tired and puzzled voice, that he had been under a spell, and that he was deeply grateful to the friend who had stopped him. He did not mention the south again that evening, nor for a long time afterwards, though sometimes he looked wistfully out of the window.

Mole was wise enough not to argue about the sea, and instead he quietly put a pencil and a sheet of paper into Rat's paws and suggested that the swallows and the harbours might make a fine poem. Rat looked at him for a moment, then began to write, slowly at first and then faster and faster. Soon the verses were pouring onto the page, and the restless ache in his heart seemed to pour out with them.

In the days that followed, Rat grew steadily more cheerful, and the strange longing faded until it seemed no more than a dream. The two friends spent cosy autumn evenings beside the fire, with the rain tapping at the window and the lamp burning softly, while Rat read his new poems aloud and Mole listened and nodded with solemn approval. Neither of them guessed that a visitor was already on his way, wet, weary and ashamed.

One wild, wet night, when the wind was howling round the bank and the rain hammered on the roof, the friends were thinking of bed when a feeble knocking sounded on the front door. Rat took the lamp and opened it, and the light fell on a bent and dripping figure, plastered with mud from head to foot and so ragged that he hardly seemed an animal at all. For a long moment nobody spoke, and the rain dripped from the stranger's nose onto the doormat.

Then Rat gasped, for under the mud, the rags and a bonnet that had once been respectable, he recognised a face that he had thought he would never see again. It was Toad, thin and weary and shaking with cold, and he asked in a feeble voice whether his old friend would let him in, though he had no right to expect it. Rat's heart softened at once, and without another word he pulled the shivering wanderer inside and shut the stormy night out.

Rat gave him dry clothes, a hot bath and a bowl of steaming soup, and after an hour by the fire Toad had recovered so much of his spirits that he could not resist telling his story. He bragged of the dungeon, of the washerwoman's gown, of the engine and the barge, and of the horse that he had sold to the gipsy, and his chest swelled more with each adventure. Rat, who had been listening with a face like a stone, finally raised a paw and told him to stop at once.

Rat told him sternly that there was nothing whatever to be proud of, and that the whole business had been folly from beginning to end. Then, more gently, he said that there was something Toad did not know, and that it was the worst news he had ever had to give. While Toad had been away in prison and on the road, a terrible thing had happened to his house.

Rat explained that, when Toad had been sent to prison, the weasels, stoats and ferrets of the Wild Wood had seen their chance and marched into Toad Hall. They had turned out the servants and taken possession of the whole house, and they were living there still, eating Toad's food, sleeping in his beds and boasting to every passer-by that the place now belonged to them. Toad listened with growing horror, and the colour drained from his face until he looked as pale as a sheet of paper.

Toad leapt to his feet with blazing eyes, snatched up a poker and announced that he would march to the Hall that very moment and drive out every thief and robber single-handed. Rat caught his arm and pulled him back into his chair, reminding him that the Wild Wooders were many, that they were armed and that every gate and window of the Hall was watched day and night. It was no time for noise and heroics, he said, but for cool thought and careful planning, and for the advice of somebody wiser than either of them.

At last the fight went out of him, and Toad sank back into the chair and wept bitterly, declaring that he was the most foolish and ungrateful animal that had ever lived, and that he deserved everything he had suffered. Rat and Mole exchanged a glance, for they had heard such speeches before, but this time there was something real in his sorrow. Rat said quietly that in the morning they would send for Badger, who always knew what to do.

The next morning Badger arrived at Rat's house, having been fetched by Mole at first light, and he stood in the doorway and looked at Toad for a long time without speaking. Toad, wrapped in a borrowed dressing gown and sitting very small at the breakfast table, hung his head, for he knew that there were a great many things that Badger had a right to say. The silence stretched out so long that the toast went cold on the plate, and the clock on the mantelpiece seemed to tick louder and louder.

At last Badger said, in a deep and weary voice, that Toad had been a great fool, that every one of his misfortunes was of his own making and that he ought to be heartily ashamed of himself. Then his stern face relaxed, and he took Toad's paw in his own and said that the past was the past, and that a toad who had been through so much deserved another chance. Toad blew his nose loudly and mumbled that he did not deserve such friends.

Rat told Badger everything he had learned about the Wild Wooders in Toad Hall: how many of them there were, how they kept armed sentries at every gate and how they feasted every night on Toad's food. Badger listened with his paws behind his back, nodding slowly, and then he asked Toad to draw a rough plan of the house and grounds on the back of an old envelope. Toad, glad to be of some use at last, set to work at once and drew a plan so careful that even Badger was impressed.

Badger studied the plan for a long time in silence, and then he said that they could never take the Hall by force, for the Wild Wooders were too many and too well armed. A sly smile crept over his broad face as he added that he knew something about Toad Hall that nobody else remembered, and that it might be worth more than a hundred soldiers. The three friends leaned closer over the table, hardly daring to breathe, while a log settled in the grate with a soft sigh.

Badger explained that a secret tunnel began on the river bank, not far from Toad's own boathouse, and ran for a long way beneath the fields and the garden, until it came up under the floor of the Hall itself. Toad's father, a most respectable old animal, had shown it to Badger years ago and had made him promise never to tell his careless son, who might have boasted of it to every passer-by. Toad opened his mouth to protest, thought better of it, blushed deeply and closed it again without a word.

Badger said that before anything else they must find out what the Wild Wooders were doing inside the Hall and how well they kept their guard. Mole, who had been silent until now, bravely offered to go and see for himself, and he put on the washerwoman's crumpled gown and bonnet that Toad had worn, laughing at himself in the glass. Rat could not help smiling at the sight, but he squeezed his friend's shoulder in warm admiration, for he knew how brave the shy little Mole had become.

Carrying a basket on his arm, Mole walked up the long drive of Toad Hall with an air of calm respectability, and he looked so exactly like an honest old washerwoman that nobody suspected him. At the gate, a pair of stoats with sticks stepped out of a hole in the wall and demanded roughly to know who he was and what he wanted. Mole said in a quavering voice that he was only the washerwoman, come to ask for the Hall's linen.

The stoats roared with laughter at the idea of a washerwoman in such a place, and one of them told her to go round to the kitchen door and bother the cook. As Mole turned away, he pricked up his ears, for the sentries were gossiping among themselves. He heard them say that Toad was a fool who would never be seen again, and that the Chief Weasel was giving a grand banquet in the hall that very night.

From a quiet corner of the garden Mole watched lanterns glitter in every window, while weasels, stoats and ferrets in their best finery hurried up the steps, shouting and laughing as they went. He counted as many as he could, noted that most of them carried no weapon but a knife and fork, and slipped away through a gap in the hedge before anyone could ask more questions. All the way home he rehearsed his report to himself, like a schoolboy preparing to recite a poem before a very strict teacher.

Mole hurried back to Rat's house, flung off the bonnet and poured out his news to Badger, Rat and Toad, who listened without a word, hanging on every detail. When he had finished, Badger rubbed his paws together with a satisfied growl and declared that no better chance would ever come, for the whole gang would be shut in the banqueting hall, stuffing themselves, with their weapons laid aside. That very night, he said, they would go down the secret tunnel and take Toad Hall back.

That evening Badger opened a long chest and handed out the weapons, giving each of the friends a stout club, a cutlass and a pair of pistols, with handcuffs and bandages in case of trouble. Toad, swinging his club at an imaginary enemy, nearly knocked the lamp off the table, and Badger told him sharply to keep it pointed at the floor. The old animal was calm, but his eyes glittered like a soldier's before a battle.

Badger insisted that they should all lie down and rest until dusk, since a tired soldier makes a poor fighter, and the three friends stretched out on the sofas while the old animal sat watching the clock. Toad, who could not remain silent for two minutes together, kept sitting up to describe how bravely he would fight and how many weasels he would capture. In the end, even Toad's snores filled the room, and the others smiled in the firelight.

At dusk Badger woke them, and the four friends slipped out of the house and set off in single file along the river bank, Badger leading and Toad bringing up the rear with his club on his shoulder. Not a word was spoken, and the only sounds were the sigh of the wind in the willows, the gurgle of the river and the faint crunch of their feet on the gravel. A pale moon was rising over the meadows as they passed, and the whole countryside seemed to hold its breath.

Not far from Toad's boathouse, Badger halted beside an ancient willow and pushed aside a curtain of ivy and roots to reveal a low, dark opening, so well hidden that none of them would ever have found it. He lit a small lantern, put his finger to his lips and crawled inside, and one by one the others followed him into the darkness. Behind them the river chuckled quietly, as though it too were in the secret.

The tunnel was narrow and low, and so damp that water dripped steadily from the roof onto their heads and ran in cold trickles down their necks. They were obliged to walk almost bent double, with the lantern throwing wild shadows on the walls, and it seemed to Mole that they had been plodding for hours before the passage began to climb. Toad groaned, shivered and wished aloud that he were at home, until Badger told him to be quiet.

At last the tunnel ended at a short flight of rough steps, and above them, in the roof, they could see the faint outline of a trapdoor with a thin line of yellow light around its edge. From the other side came a muffled roar of voices, shouting, singing and laughter, and the clatter of plates and mugs, as though the whole population of the Wild Wood were being fed at once. The four friends stood very still in the dripping dark and listened with beating hearts, waiting for the moment when they would be needed.

Then, one by one, they began to make out words, and they heard the Chief Weasel proposing toasts to the cleverness of the Wild Wooders and the stupidity of their former owner. The guests roared and drummed on the tables, and a rude song about Toad followed, with a chorus about a vain old fool who lost his house, bellowed out by dozens of throats. Badger put a heavy paw on Toad's shoulder and held it there firmly, as one might hold down a kettle that is about to boil over.

Toad shook with rage from the tips of his ears to the tips of his toes, and for one dreadful moment he looked as though he might burst through the trapdoor alone and spoil everything. Badger's grip tightened, and in a fierce whisper he reminded Toad that a battle was won by waiting for the right moment. Toad swallowed hard and nodded, though his eyes were still blazing and his club trembled in his paws like a leaf in a high wind.

In the flickering lantern light Badger gave his last orders in a whisper that the three friends could hardly hear. When he gave the signal, they must burst up through the trapdoor together, each shouting at the top of his voice, so that the enemy would never guess how few they were. Rat and Mole nodded grimly, and Toad gripped his club until his knuckles went white.

Badger drew a deep breath, planted his broad back against the trapdoor and, with a bellow that shook the tunnel, heaved it open. A blaze of light and a roar of astonished voices fell upon them as they swarmed up the steps, and for one instant the entire banqueting hall seemed frozen in surprise. Then Toad's war cry rose above everything else, and the battle for Toad Hall began.

The four friends burst up through the floor of the banqueting hall, shouting and brandishing their clubs, and the astonished weasels dropped their forks, their mugs and their dignity in a single moment of panic. Tables crashed over, plates and bottles smashed on the flagstones, and the great hall rang with shrieks of terror, as the guests believed that an army had risen out of the earth. For a few glorious seconds, in all the smoke and the shouting, nobody knew who was attacking whom.

Badger bellowed like a bull and laid about him with his heavy club, while Rat and Mole, side by side, charged through the crowd with their cutlasses raised and their eyes alight. Toad, leaping onto the table among the broken dishes, swung his club in great circles and shrieked that he was the terror of the river, that he was Toad the Terrible and that nobody could escape him. Even in the middle of all that uproar, he was thoroughly enjoying himself, and he would remember every moment of it for years.

The weasels, stoats and ferrets fled in all directions at once, hurling themselves through the windows, diving under the tables and scrambling up the great chimney in a rain of soot. In the dreadful confusion, every one of them believed that the hall was full of enemies, and not one stopped to count how few there were. The Chief Weasel himself was seen leaping over a sideboard with his napkin still tucked into his collar.

The Chief Weasel leapt onto a chair and tried to rally his followers, shrieking that they outnumbered their enemies ten to one, but nobody stopped to listen. A whistling club knocked the chair from under him, and he was swept helplessly toward the door by the stream of running animals, protesting and spluttering all the way. Not many minutes earlier, he had been the proudest and most swaggering creature in the whole of that great crowded room.

Toad, drunk with victory, rampaged through the hall like a one-animal army, whacking at every tail he could reach and shouting his own name in a terrible voice that cracked at the high notes. Mole had to duck twice to avoid the sweep of his club, and Rat, laughing helplessly, begged him to remember that it was only the weasels who were supposed to be hit. Even Badger's stern old face twitched with amusement, though he shouted at Toad to stop before somebody was really hurt.

Outside, in the dark garden, the sentries at the gates heard the uproar and saw their frightened comrades streaming past, and they quickly concluded that a great army had arrived by magic. They threw down their sticks and took to their heels, and the last of the Wild Wooders vanished into the night, running for the safety of the Wild Wood as fast as their legs could carry them. Behind them the lights of Toad Hall blazed out in every window, as though the old house were welcoming its own back.

When the noise had died away, a handful of weasels were found under the tables, too frightened to run, and they stood up trembling with their paws in the air, begging for mercy. Badger looked them over with his fierce old eyes, then said that he would spare them if they cleaned up the mess, swore never to return and promised to behave for the rest of their lives. They agreed with indecent speed and set to work with brooms and buckets, sweeping up the wreckage of the great feast.

When it was all over, the four friends stood in the middle of the wrecked banqueting hall, panting and dishevelled and grinning at each other like schoolboys. They counted their injuries and found only a few bruises, a torn sleeve and a singed whisker, and they realised with astonishment that they had won a great victory without losing a single member of their party. Toad Hall, empty and silent among the ruins of the feast, was theirs again.

Toad walked slowly through his own house with a lamp in his paw, past stained carpets, torn curtains, broken furniture and walls that had been scribbled on, and he felt a pang in his heart at every ruined room. The Wild Wooders had lived there for weeks like a plague of locusts, but the great house itself still stood, solid and welcoming. He said aloud, with a break in his voice, that it was good to be home.

Badger declared that they had all earned a night's rest, and that the cleaning and the counting of losses could wait until the morning. The four friends carried candles up the great staircase, found four clean beds that the weasels had somehow overlooked and sank gratefully between the sheets. Within minutes the only sounds in the whole of Toad Hall were the creak of old beams and the contented snores of its heroes.

In the clear light of morning the four friends came down the great staircase and saw by daylight how much damage the Wild Wooders had done. The windows were broken, the carpets stained and burnt, the walls scribbled upon and the kitchen full of mountains of dirty dishes, and Rat remarked with a sigh that it would take weeks to put things right. Toad, however, only said cheerfully that servants were a marvellous invention, and that somebody would surely be along to deal with it all.

News of the great victory spread quickly through the countryside, and before noon Toad's old servants came hurrying back from the cottages and farms where they had taken shelter, weeping with joy and carrying brooms, buckets and baskets of provisions. The housekeeper took command of the kitchen, the butler counted the silver with trembling paws, and the whole house echoed with the sounds of scrubbing, hammering and singing. By the time the lamps were lit that evening, the worst of the mess had gone, and the old house looked like itself again.

That evening Toad announced that he would give a grand banquet to thank all his friends and neighbours, and Badger, after a moment's thought, agreed on one condition. There was to be no boasting, no long speeches and no songs in praise of Toad's cleverness, and he must remember always that the real heroes of the story were his friends. Toad opened his mouth to protest, then closed it again, thought hard for a long moment and nodded slowly.

Toad sat down at his desk to write the invitations, and the first card he composed was crammed with magnificent adjectives about the Toad of Toad Hall, the hero of the hour, the captain of the battle. Then he caught Badger's eye across the room, tore the card into little pieces and wrote another, plain and friendly, that said only that Toad would be glad if his friends would dine with him. It was the hardest piece of writing he had ever done, and he finished it with a groan.

Then, to the surprise of his friends, Toad remembered the kind people who had helped him during his flight, and he sat down to write grateful letters and to pack presents for the jailer's daughter and the engine driver. He even sent a generous payment to the barge woman to make up for her stolen horse and her spoiled washing. It was a strange new feeling, to be grateful, and he found that he rather liked it.

On the night of the banquet the great hall was clean, polished and hung with glowing lanterns, and the long table groaned under dishes of every kind that the cook had been able to find. Otter and his son Portly arrived first, followed by the field mice with their red scarves, the two young hedgehogs and many other friends of the river bank, all eager to hear the story of the battle. Toad stood at the door, bowing politely to each guest like the humblest of hosts.

During the dinner Toad said very little, though several times he felt his old boasts rising in his throat, and each time he swallowed them down and took another sip of water. When it was time for a toast, he rose and spoke only a few simple words, thanking Badger, Rat and Mole by name for saving his home and, he added, for teaching him a lesson he would never forget. The guests, who had expected a long speech, cheered him louder than if he had talked for an hour.

From that evening Toad was a changed animal, quieter, kinder and wiser than he had ever been before, and the river bank was astonished at the improvement. Whenever he felt one of his old crazes rising inside him, he thought of the cold dungeon, the barge woman's tub and the faces of his friends in the tunnel, and the feeling gradually passed. It was said that he never boasted again, or at least never for longer than a minute.

The Wild Wooders never forgot the night when four animals burst up through the floor of Toad Hall and put a crowd of them to flight. From then on they treated Badger and his friends with deep respect, and it is said that a naughty weasel child needed only to hear that Badger was coming to fall silent at once. The Wild Wood, which had once frightened Mole so badly, became a much friendlier place.

Mole and Rat returned to their quiet days of boating, picnics and evenings by the fire, with Badger calling more often than before and Toad, a new animal, joining their walks. The seasons turned as they always do, from spring to summer, from autumn to snow, and the river rolled on beneath the willows as it had always done. Mole, looking at it one evening, thought that of all the places in the Wide World, none could be more beautiful than home.
